x: Home › Verses Verse a Day #1 · October 12, 2026 John 1:1 Alignment: 5/5 for the words, 4/5 for nuance Four witnesses Greek · SBLGNT Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. En archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos. Latin · Vulgate In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum. KJV In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. ESV In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Key words logos → Verbum → Word. Logos means "word," and also reason or the ordering principle of the universe in Greek philosophy. Jerome's Verbum keeps "word" but loses the "reason" side. English follows the Latin. archē → principio → beginning. "En archē" echoes Genesis 1:1 in the Greek Septuagint (Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεός). The Vulgate's Genesis likewise starts "In principio." All three languages keep that echo. pros ton theon → apud Deum → with God. Pros suggests being "toward" or "face to face with" someone. Apud means "in the presence of," and "with" is the flattest of the three. theos with and without "the." The Greek has ton theon ("the God") in clause 2 but theos with no article in clause 3, placed first for emphasis. Grammarians (Colwell's rule, Harner 1973) read the bare theos as describing what the Word is: fully divine in nature, but not the same person as "the God" just mentioned. That is why "the Word was God" is the standard reading.

d: Thy kingdom come
x: Home › Verses Verse a Day #4 · October 15, 2026 Matthew 6:10 Alignment: Some drift Setting the scene Same hillside above the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, around AD 28–30, still early in Jesus' Galilean ministry and still in the Sermon on the Mount. The disciples and the crowd have just heard him teach them to start prayer with "Our Father." Now come the next two lines. These listeners live under Rome: Herod Antipas holds Galilee for Caesar, and many Jews longed for a Davidic Messiah who would restore Israel's kingdom and push the empire out. First-century prayers and writings (like the Psalms of Solomon) asked God to raise up that king. So when a young rabbi from Nazareth tells them to pray "Your kingdom come," they would have heard something electric. He does not name a rebel army or a throne in Jerusalem. He asks them to want God's reign, and God's will, the way heaven already has it, right here on the ground where Roman boots still walk. d: Forgive us our debts
x: Home › Verses Verse a Day #6 · October 17, 2026 Matthew 6:12 Alignment: Close, with a tense difference Setting the scene Still on the hillside above the Sea of Galilee near Capernaum, around AD 28–30, in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has taught his followers to ask for God's name to be honored, his kingdom to come, and bread for today. Now he turns to debt, a word his listeners felt in their bones. Under Roman rule, Galilean farmers paid tribute to Rome, taxes to Herod Antipas, and tithes to the Temple, and a bad harvest could push a family into loans they could never repay. Debtors could lose their land or even be sold into servitude. The Law of Moses promised a release of debts every seventh year (Deuteronomy 15), but by Jesus' day lenders often sidestepped it with a legal device called the prosbul, credited to Rabbi Hillel. Many hoped the Messiah would bring a true jubilee and wipe the slate clean. A young rabbi from Nazareth tells them to ask God to cancel their debts, and in the same breath ties that request to canceling the debts others owe them. He speaks as a man in the flesh to people who did not yet know who was standing in front of them. d: God with us

Joseph, a builder, is betrothed to a young woman named Mary. In Jewish custom a betrothal was already a binding marriage contract; only a divorce could end it, even before the couple lived together. Then Mary is found to be with child, and Joseph, "a just man," plans to end things quietly so she will not be shamed (Matthew 1:19). An angel stops him in a dream: the child is from the Holy Spirit, and his name will be Jesus, "for he shall save his people from their sins" (1:21). Matthew then steps back and tells his readers what this means. He reaches about 700 years into Israel's past, to the prophet Isaiah standing before King Ahaz of Judah around 735 BC, when Jerusalem was terrified of an invasion by the kings of Aram and Israel. Isaiah offered the king a sign: a child called Immanuel, "God with us." Matthew says that sign comes to its full meaning in the baby Joseph will name Jesus. There is no room for them in the guest room, so Mary lays her newborn son in a manger, a feeding trough for animals (Luke 2:7). Yet they are the first to hear. An angel of the Lord appears, the glory of the Lord shines around them, and they are terrified. "Fear not," the angel says, "for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy" (2:10): a Savior, Christ the Lord, has been born in the city of David. It is the farthest north Jesus is recorded taking his disciples, and it is pagan ground. A huge wall of rock rises over a spring that feeds the Jordan River, and in the cliff face is a dark cave the locals treated as a gateway to the underworld. Shrines to the Greek god Pan were cut into the rock, Herod the Great had built a white marble temple to Caesar Augustus nearby, and Herod's son Philip renamed the town Caesarea in honor of the emperor. Here, surrounded by rival gods and emperors, Jesus asks, "Who do people say that the Son of Man is?" Then, more pointedly: "But who do you say that I am?" Simon answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (16:16). Jesus calls him blessed, because this was revealed to him by the Father, not by flesh and blood. John the Baptist has just been arrested by Herod Antipas, and Jesus, freshly back from forty days of testing in the wilderness, leaves his hometown of Nazareth and settles in Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. Matthew sees in this move the fulfillment of Isaiah: "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light" (Matthew 4:15–16; Isaiah 9:1–2). The kingdom of Portugal itself took shape in the 12th century, and its kings and queens kept close ties with the shrine. Deep Dive History and origins In the early Middle Ages the Christian kingdoms of northern Spain held a narrow strip between the mountains and the sea, and pilgrims often followed the coast, where the roads were safer. Many arrived by sea at Cantabrian ports. As the Reconquista pushed south and the Francés became the main road in the 11th–12th centuries, the coastal way became less used, but it never disappeared: monasteries, hospitals and churches dedicated to St James line it. In 2015 UNESCO extended the Camino's World Heritage listing to the "Routes of Northern Spain", including the Norte. Regions crossed The Norte crosses four regions: the Basque Country (Gipuzkoa and Bizkaia), Cantabria , Asturias and Galicia . Deep Dive History and origins According to tradition, King Alfonso II of Asturias ("the Chaste"), ruling from Oviedo, travelled to see the newly discovered tomb of St James in the 820s or early 830s (the earliest surviving charter mentioning the discovery dates from 834) and ordered the first church built there, making him the first pilgrim of all. That he promoted the cult and endowed the church is supported by early documents; that he walked this exact route is tradition. Deep Dive History and origins From the 12th century pilgrims from England, Ireland, Scotland, Flanders and Scandinavia sailed to Galicia and landed at A Coruña or Ferrol , then walked the remaining distance inland. English royal records from the 14th and 15th centuries include licences for ships to carry pilgrims to Santiago, especially in Holy Years: in 1434 licences were issued for dozens of ships, recorded in Rymer's Foedera . Sea travel was quicker than crossing France but brought its own dangers; an anonymous late-medieval English poem about seasick pilgrims ( The Pilgrims' Sea Voyage ) begins, memorably, "Men may leve all gamys / That saylen to seynt Jamys". Long stages between villages and extreme summer heat in Extremadura. About half of its pilgrims actually start in Ourense (~105 km) and only one in five from Seville. Good to know Best seasons: spring and autumn. Avoid June to August in the south. Fly into Seville (SVQ). Deep Dive History and origins The route follows much of the Roman road that linked Emerita Augusta (Mérida) with Asturica Augusta (Astorga), whose stations are recorded in the Roman Antonine Itinerary (generally dated to the 3rd century), though not as a single named road. Roman milestones still stand along it. The name has nothing to do with silver as far as anyone can prove: a traditional explanation derives "Plata" from the Arabic balat (paved road), but scholars do not agree, and other proposals include the Latin delapidata ("paved with stone"). In the Middle Ages, Christians living under Muslim rule (Mozarabs) and later southern pilgrims used it to go north. d: The pilgrim passport and the certificate: the exact rules
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Camino de Santiago Credencial & Compostela The pilgrim passport and the certificate: the exact rules The credencial The credencial is your pilgrim passport. You collect stamps ( sellos ) in it from albergues, churches, cafés and town halls. It is required to sleep in pilgrim albergues and to claim the Compostela. Only the Cathedral's official credencial, or one from an organisation it authorises, is accepted. In the US you can get one from American Pilgrims on the Camino ; in Santiago, from the Pilgrim Office. The Compostela: official requirements The Pilgrim's Reception Office states ( official page , checked Oct 15, 2026): - On foot or horseback: at least 100 continuous km on the same recognised route , and the final stage must be the one that leads into Santiago's Cathedral. - By bicycle: at least 200 km under the same conditions. - Started outside Spain on a recognised route: at least 70 km in Spain. - Stamps: at least two stamps per day over the qualifying distance ( Pilgrim Office FAQ ). If you walk in sections, stamp at the start and end of each stage with the date. - It is given to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons. A separate Certificate of Distance is available for a small fee. Safe starting points: Sarria (Francés), Tui (Portugués), Ferrol (Inglés), or further back. d: From a hermit's star to half a million pilgrims
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Camino de Santiago History From a hermit's star to half a million pilgrims History. St James the Greater, one of the Twelve, was martyred in Jerusalem around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). In the early 9th century a tomb near Iria Flavia was identified as his, and King Alfonso II of Asturias came from Oviedo to visit it, the journey later remembered as the Camino Primitivo. A church, and later the Romanesque cathedral, rose over the site. The 12th-century Codex Calixtinus included a guide for pilgrims on the French Way. After centuries of decline the pilgrimage revived in the late 20th century: the Camino Francés became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and the northern routes were added in 2015 ( UNESCO ). Pilgrim numbers grew from a few thousand to 530,987 in 2025. Legend. Tradition holds that James preached in Hispania and that, after his martyrdom, his disciples brought his body by stone boat to Galicia. Centuries later a hermit named Pelayo saw a star or lights over a field. That's one popular explanation for Compostela , "field of the star" (scholars also propose compositum , "burial place"). The scallop shell, gathered on Galician beaches, became the pilgrim's badge. Sources UNESCO: Routes of Santiago de Compostela Oficina del Peregrino: history of the Compostela Gronze: Camino Francés overview Last verified: October 15, 2026. x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Michael's Line Skellig Michael Sceilg Mhichíl, Co. Kerry, Ireland Country Ireland Type Island monastery UNESCO 1996 Season ~May–Sept History. A jagged sea rock off the Iveragh Peninsula holds one of the best-preserved early Christian monasteries in Europe: drystone beehive huts and oratories built by monks who lived there for centuries in the early Middle Ages. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 ( UNESCO ). Legend. In one tradition, St Michael appeared here to help St Patrick drive the serpents and demons out of Ireland. The rock in depth Founding stories: legend and history History or legend? Nobody knows when the monastery was founded or by whom. UNESCO says plainly that "the date of the foundation of the monastery on this island is not known", and it puts the dedication to St Michael somewhere between 950 and 1050. The stories of a 6th-century founder and of a drowned prince are tradition, not record. The legend. Local tradition names St Fionán as the founder, a 6th-century monk said to have rowed out from the Iveragh coast with a few companions. There are several saints called Fionán in Irish tradition, and none of them can be firmly tied to Skellig. An older story, from the medieval Lebor Gabála Érenn ("Book of Invasions"), says the rock was the grave of Ir , a son of Míl, drowned when the sons of Míl invaded Ireland. A tidal island crowned by a castle and church. In the Middle Ages it was a priory of the Benedictine abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel, until England dissolved its "alien priories" in 1414. It later became a fortress. Colonel John St Aubyn bought it in 1659, and his family still lives in the castle. In 1954 the 3rd Lord St Levan gave most of the island to the National Trust, and the family kept a 999-year lease to live there. Legend. Fishermen are said to have seen St Michael standing on the rock (traditionally in AD 495). Cornish folklore also says the giant Cormoran lived here until Jack the Giant Killer defeated him. One of the oldest shrines to St Michael in the West: a natural cave on the Gargano promontory, venerated since late antiquity. It was a major sanctuary of the Lombards and a great medieval pilgrim goal, where Crusaders and pilgrims stopped on their way to the Apulian ports. Since 2011 it has been part of the UNESCO site "The Longobards in Italy: Places of Power" ( UNESCO ). Legend. According to the Liber de apparitione , Michael appeared to the Bishop of Siponto in the 490s and later declared that he had consecrated the cave himself, so it's called the "Celestial Basilica" that was never consecrated by human hands. The main pilgrimage site of the Dodecanese, set on a quiet bay in the south of Symi. The monastery is documented in the 15th century. It was destroyed in the mid-18th century and rebuilt in 1783 , when the present church ( katholikon ) and its frescoes were made. It is famous for its huge icon of the Archangel Michael, covered in silver in 1724 and honoured by sailors. Who painted the icon, and when, is unknown ( Visit Greece ). Legend. The icon was found here and, the story goes, kept returning to this spot whenever it was moved, so the monastery was built where it chose to stay. Sailors once sent offerings floating in bottles that the current carried to the monastery. Note: Panormitis is an Orthodox monastery. Visitors should dress modestly (covered shoulders and knees). d: Seven sanctuaries of the Archangel, from Ireland to the Holy Land
x: Home › Pilgrimage St Michael's Line Seven sanctuaries of the Archangel, from Ireland to the Holy Land "Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon" (Revelation 12:7, ESV). Across Europe and the Mediterranean, Christians built shrines to the Archangel Michael on rocks, islands and mountaintops. Seven of the most famous are often said to lie on a single straight line. The legend of the line. A popular modern story says these seven sanctuaries form a perfect line, the stroke of Michael's sword as he drove the devil into hell, and that it lines up with the summer-solstice sunset. It's a lovely image, but it is folklore, not history . On a globe the sites don't sit on a single straight (great-circle) line; they only look aligned on flat Mercator-style maps, with gaps of tens of kilometres, and the solstice claim doesn't hold up either ( analysis , Italian study ). What's true. Each sanctuary is real, ancient and beloved, and devotion to St Michael genuinely connects them: Mont-Saint-Michel and St Michael's Mount were linked by monks, and Monte Sant'Angelo inspired the Norman shrine. That's a pilgrimage worth making, line or no line. The seven sanctuaries Skellig Michael Sceilg Mhichíl, Co. The inscription on its façade calls it omnium urbis et orbis ecclesiarum mater et caput : "mother and head of all the churches of the city and the world." Across the square is one of Rome's most moving devotions, the Scala Santa , the "Holy Stairs," which pilgrims climb on their knees. Good to know Entry to the basilica is free; the cloister has a small fee. The Scala Santa is climbed only on the knees, praying; it's free, and side staircases let you walk up. The Sancta Sanctorum chapel at the top is visible through grilles, with a paid entry to go inside. Getting there: Metro A to San Giovanni . On the walk it is about 4 km from San Sebastiano and 1 km from Santa Croce. Feast: the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, 9 November , is a feast for the whole Latin Church. x: Home › Pilgrimage › Rome and the Seven Churches Santa Croce in Gerusalemme Station 5 · Holy Cross in Jerusalem, the relics of the Passion Photo: 05 Facade Santa Croce Gerusalemme by NateBergin, CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Station 5 of 7 Rank Minor basilica Founded c. 320s Relics chapel Closed for works (2026) The name is not a mistake. This church was meant to be a piece of Jerusalem in Rome : built in the palace of St Helena , Constantine's mother, to hold the relics of Christ's Passion she brought back from the Holy Land, its floor was laid, so the story goes, on earth from Calvary. Relics chapel closed. As of October 2026 the basilica's official site says the Chapel of the Relics is closed for urgent building works by order of the Vicariate of Rome and the Ministry of Culture, with the reopening date to be announced on the site. The basilica is open. Check before you go . Good to know Hours (official site): basilica 7:30–19:00; museum 10:00–12:00 and 16:00–17:30, entered from the sacristy. Entry is free. The relics chapel , when open, is free; it's closed to visits during Masses. Getting there: tram 3 or 8, or a 10-minute walk from Metro A San Giovanni . Deep Dive History History. In the early 4th century Helena lived in the Sessorian Palace , an imperial residence on this spot. d: Station 6 · St Lawrence Outside the Walls, the deacon martyr's tomb
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Rome and the Seven Churches San Lorenzo fuori le mura Station 6 · St Lawrence Outside the Walls, the deacon martyr's tomb Photo: San Lorenzo fuori le mura - facade by Unknown author, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Station 6 of 7 Rank Papal minor basilica Martyr Lawrence, AD 258 Entry Free St Lawrence was one of the seven deacons of Rome, keeper of the Church's goods and its care for the poor, martyred in August 258 under Valerian. His tomb on the Via Tiburtina became one of the most visited shrines in Rome. The basilica over it is really two churches joined end to end , and in 1943 it became the only papal basilica struck in World War II. Good to know Entry is free; the Romanesque cloister is opened by the Capuchin friars at set times. Getting there: tram 2, 3, 8 or 19, or bus 71 and 492, to Verano . On the walk it is 2 km from Santa Croce and 2.5 km to Santa Maria Maggiore. Feast: 10 August. Romans say the August shooting stars (the Perseids) are "Lawrence's tears." Next door is the Verano , Rome's monumental 19th-century cemetery, worth a slow walk. Deep Dive History: two basilicas made one History. Constantine built a large funerary basilica near the catacomb of Cyriaca, where Lawrence was buried. Pope Pelagius II (579–590) built a smaller church right over the tomb, cut into the hillside; its triumphal arch mosaic shows Pelagius offering the church to Christ. x: Home › Pilgrimage › Rome and the Seven Churches Santa Maria Maggiore Station 7 · St Mary Major, Our Lady of the Snows and the Salus Populi Romani Photo: Roma - 2016-05-23 - Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore - 2957 by Pierre-Selim Huard, CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Station 7 of 7 Rank Papal major basilica Built 432–440 Bell tower 75 m, tallest in Rome The walk ends with Mary. Santa Maria Maggiore , on the top of the Esquiline Hill, is the largest and oldest of Rome's churches dedicated to the Mother of God, and the only one of the four papal basilicas whose 5th-century structure still stands. It keeps the beloved icon of the Salus Populi Romani , "Protectress of the Roman People," and since April 2025 it is also the burial place of Pope Francis . Good to know Entry is free. The museum, the loggia mosaics and the bell tower have paid guided visits. Getting there: a 5-minute walk from Termini (Metro A and B); Metro B Cavour is also close. Pope Francis's tomb is in the left aisle near the Pauline Chapel, under a plain slab inscribed simply Franciscus . Expect a queue. 5 August , the feast of Our Lady of the Snows: white petals are released from the ceiling of the Pauline Chapel during Mass. Deep Dive History History. d: The Sette Chiese walk of St Philip Neri: seven basilicas, one day, about 25 km
x: Home › Pilgrimage Rome and the Seven Churches The Sette Chiese walk of St Philip Neri: seven basilicas, one day, about 25 km Photo: Basilica di San Pietro in Vaticano September 2015-1a by Alvesgaspar, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Once a year, and in Holy Years far more often, Romans and pilgrims set out before dawn to walk to seven great churches in a single day: the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul , the catacomb shrine of St Sebastian , the Pope's cathedral of St John Lateran , the Passion relics of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme , the martyr's tomb of St Lawrence , and the great Marian basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore . The walk is about 20 to 25 km, and its modern form was given to it in the 1550s by a cheerful Florentine priest, St Philip Neri , the "Apostle of Rome." Good to know Distance and time: about 20–25 km depending on the streets you choose; allow 10–12 hours with time inside each church. Starting at Philip Neri's own church, Santa Maria in Vallicella (the Chiesa Nuova ), is a nice touch. Dress code: shoulders and knees covered in every basilica; St Peter's enforces it at security. d: "A citizen of no obscure city": Paul's birthplace in Cilicia
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Footsteps of St Paul Tarsus "A citizen of no obscure city": Paul's birthplace in Cilicia Photo: Cleopatra's Gate, Tarsus, Mersin Province by Nedim Ardoğa, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Country Türkiye Province Mersin Acts 9:11, 30; 21:39; 22:3 Nearest airport Adana (ADA) "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city" (Acts 21:39, ESV). Paul was proud of his hometown, and rightly: Tarsus was a rich trading city at the foot of the Taurus Mountains, on the river Cydnus, famed for its schools of philosophy. Today it's a busy Turkish town of about 350,000, with a few precious traces of the city Paul knew. Good to know Getting there: Tarsus is 40 km from Adana airport and 30 km from Mersin, with frequent trains and buses. St Paul's Church is a state museum; Christian groups may celebrate Mass with permission arranged in advance through the local Catholic church. The Catholic Apostolic Vicariate of Anatolia keeps a small presence here. Feast: pilgrims gather on and around 29 June , the feast of Sts Peter and Paul. Deep Dive Paul's city History. Tarsus was capital of the Roman province of Cilicia . Here, in 41 BC , Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus in her gilded barge to meet Mark Antony. The geographer Strabo , a near-contemporary of Paul, wrote that the people of Tarsus were so devoted to learning that they surpassed even Athens and Alexandria. d: Where the disciples were first called Christians, and where every journey began
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Footsteps of St Paul Antioch Where the disciples were first called Christians, and where every journey began Photo: Antakya Church of St. Peter exterior ın 2025 05 by Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Country Türkiye Today Antakya, Hatay Acts 11:19–30; 13:1–3; 14:26–15:35; 18:22 Rebuilding After 2023 quake Antioch on the Orontes was the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, a capital of perhaps a quarter of a million people. Here the Gospel was first preached widely to non-Jews, and "in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians" (Acts 11:26, ESV). It was Paul's home church: each of his three journeys started here. After the earthquakes. The earthquakes of 6 February 2023 devastated Antakya, killing tens of thousands across the region and destroying much of the old city. The cave Church of St Peter on the mountainside survived with damage. Check the current situation and opening times locally before you travel. Good to know Getting there: Hatay airport (HTY), about 20 km north; buses from Adana (about 3 hours). The Church of St Peter ( St. Pierre Kilisesi ) is a museum site on the slope of Mount Stauris, about 2 km north-east of the centre. Christians gather there each year on 29 June . d: Three years in the great city of Asia, and the riot in the theatre

Paul spent longer here than anywhere else on his journeys, "for three years" (Acts 20:31), and from here he wrote 1 Corinthians. Its marble streets are now the best-preserved Roman city in the eastern Mediterranean. Good to know Getting there: Selçuk is 75 km from İzmir airport by train or road; the cruise port of Kuşadası is 20 km away. Entry: the site and the Terrace Houses have separate tickets (paid, sold at the gate and online through Türkiye's museum card system). Start at the upper (Magnesia) gate and walk downhill to finish at the theatre. Go early: by mid-morning in summer the site is crowded and very hot; there's little shade. Also in Selçuk: the Basilica of St John , the column of the Artemision, the Ephesus Museum, and the House of the Virgin Mary (Meryem Ana Evi) on the mountain above. d: The first church in Europe: Lydia, the jailer, and the letter of joy
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Footsteps of St Paul Philippi The first church in Europe: Lydia, the jailer, and the letter of joy Photo: Philippi - 1 by MrPanyGoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Country Greece Near Kavala Acts 16:9–40; 20:6 UNESCO 2016 At Troas Paul had a vision in the night: a man of Macedonia urging him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us" (Acts 16:9, ESV). He sailed across, landed at Neapolis (today's Kavala) and walked up the Via Egnatia to Philippi , a proud Roman colony. Here, around AD 49–50, he founded the first Christian community in Europe, the church he would later thank in his warmest letter. Good to know Getting there: Kavala airport (KVA) is 35 km away; Philippi is 16 km from Kavala on the road to Drama, with local buses. The archaeological site (paid entry, closed some holidays) straddles the main road: the theatre, the acropolis slope and Basilica A on one side; the forum, Basilica B and the Octagon on the other. Lydia's baptistery is a 5-minute drive west at the river, in the village of Lydia. Kavala has a monument and church of St Paul by the harbour and a mosaic of his landing. x: Home › Pilgrimage › Footsteps of St Paul Thessaloniki Thessalonica: the city that heard the first letters, and the men who "turned the world upside down" Photo: Thessaloniki Saint George Rotunda from the Arch of Galerius by Ymblanter, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Country Greece Acts 17:1–10 Letters 1 & 2 Thessalonians UNESCO 1988 (monuments) From Philippi, Paul and Silas followed the Via Egnatia 150 km west to Thessalonica , capital of the province of Macedonia and a busy port. For three Sabbaths Paul argued in the synagogue that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believed, including "not a few of the leading women," but others gathered a mob and dragged Paul's host Jason before the city authorities, shouting, "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also" (Acts 17:6, ESV). Paul slipped away by night to Berea. Good to know Getting there: Thessaloniki airport (SKG) has flights from across Europe. Most sites are walkable from the waterfront. Most churches are free ; the Rotunda and the Roman forum have small fees. Byzantine churches are active Orthodox churches: dress modestly and keep quiet during services. Berea (Veria), 70 km west, has a striking Bema of St Paul , a mosaic-adorned monument at the traditional place where he preached (Acts 17:10–12). Deep Dive The earliest Christian writing History. There he gave the most famous speech of his life. The bronze plaque with the full Greek text of Paul's speech (Acts 17:22–31) is fixed to the rock at the foot of the steps. Paul arrived from Athens around AD 50, worked as a tentmaker with Priscilla and Aquila , and stayed a year and six months (Acts 18:11), longer than anywhere except Ephesus. His letters to this lively, quarrelsome church give us some of the most famous words in the Bible. Good to know Getting there: Ancient Corinth ( Archaia Korinthos ) is 80 km west of Athens, about an hour by car; trains (Proastiakos) and buses run to the modern city 7 km away. Cenchreae (Kechries), the eastern harbour, has partly submerged ruins you can see from the shore. AD 59–60 Feast 10 February After fourteen days adrift in a storm, the grain ship carrying Paul, 276 people in all, ran aground off an island. Everyone reached land. "Afterward we learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness" (Acts 28:1–2, ESV). Paul stayed three months. To the Maltese, he is their father in the faith, and the shipwreck is the founding story of one of the most Catholic countries in the world. Good to know Getting there: Malta International Airport (MLA) is 20–30 minutes by bus or taxi from Valletta and Rabat. St Paul's Grotto and the Wignacourt Museum in Rabat (paid); St Paul's Catacombs , Rabat (Heritage Malta, paid); St Paul's Shipwreck Church , Valletta (free). St Paul's Islands can be seen from the Mistra or Xemxija shore, or from summer boat trips out of Bugibba. Feast of St Paul's Shipwreck: 10 February , a public holiday with a great procession in Valletta. x: Home › Pilgrimage › Footsteps of St Paul Rome and Tre Fontane The Appian Way, two years in chains, and the place of martyrdom Photo: Tre Fontane – San Paolo -001- by Petr Adam Dohnálek, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Country Italy Acts 28:11–31 Letters Romans; prison letters Died c. AD 64–67 Paul had written to the Romans that he longed to see them (Romans 1:11). He arrived as a prisoner. Landing at Puteoli near Naples, he walked up the Appian Way , and believers came out to meet him at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns : "On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage" (Acts 28:15, ESV). Acts ends with Paul spending two whole years in Rome in his own rented lodging, under guard, "proclaiming the kingdom of God… with all boldness and without hindrance" (Acts 28:31). Good to know Tre Fontane Abbey ( Abbazia delle Tre Fontane ) is free, run by Trappist monks; the monastery shop sells their eucalyptus liqueur, chocolate and beer. Local buses, or about 30 minutes' walk from Metro B Laurentina . St Paul's tomb is at the basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls , 2.5 km north. The Mamertine Prison ( Carcere Mamertino ) by the Roman Forum is open daily with a paid multimedia visit. Rome's Seven Churches walk includes Paul's basilica as its second station. d: The Apostle to the Nations: three missionary journeys and the voyage to Rome
x: Home › Pilgrimage Footsteps of St Paul The Apostle to the Nations: three missionary journeys and the voyage to Rome Photo: The Conversion of Saint Paullabel QS:Lit,"Conversione di san Paolo"label QS:Lja, by Caravaggio, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons No one carried the Gospel further, or wrote more of the New Testament, than Paul of Tarsus . A strict Pharisee who hunted Christians, he met the risen Christ on the road to Damascus and spent the next thirty years walking and sailing some 15,000 km around the eastern Mediterranean, founding churches and writing them letters that are still read every Sunday. The Lord called him "a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles" (Acts 9:15, ESV). This guide follows him from Damascus to Rome , place by place. Good to know Two sources, read together. Our knowledge of Paul's travels comes from the Acts of the Apostles (written by Luke, probably in the 80s) and from Paul's own letters (the 50s). They mostly agree; where they differ, scholars weigh them, and we flag it. Countries today: Syria, Turkey, Cyprus, Greece, Malta, Italy and Israel. Turkey and Greece hold most of the sites; group tours often do "Seven Churches and Paul" in Turkey, or "Footsteps of Paul" in northern Greece (Kavala–Philippi–Thessaloniki–Veria) plus Athens and Corinth. d: Oslo to Trondheim: the medieval main road over Dovrefjell
x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Olav's Way Gudbrandsdalsleden Oslo to Trondheim: the medieval main road over Dovrefjell Photo: PermaLiv Gudbrandsdalen gårder 18-04-22 by Øyvind Holmstad, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Distance 643 km Days ~32 Start St Hallvard's ruins, Oslo High point ~1,300 m (Dovrefjell) The most popular of the St Olav Ways follows the medieval king's road north from Oslo : along Norway's largest lake, Mjøsa , up the long valley of Gudbrandsdalen , over the bare high plateau of Dovrefjell , and down through the forests of Trøndelag to Nidaros . It's 643 km of well-marked trail, about four to five weeks on foot at 20 km a day, and trains run beside nearly all of it, so it's easy to walk a section. Good to know Start: the ruins of St Hallvard's Cathedral in Oslo's Middelalderparken. Soon after, the route splits: west of Mjøsa via Bærum, Hadeland, Granavollen and Gjøvik, or east via Eidsvoll, Stange and Hamar. They meet again at Lillehammer . Dovrefjell: the route is "technically closed" over the mountain until about 10 June , when bridges are laid over the rivers Hondyrju and Vesle Hondyrju; snow and meltwater can last longer. If in doubt, take the train over the mountain. Pilgrim centres in Oslo, Granavollen, Hamar, Dale-Gudbrand (Hundorp), Dovrefjell and Trondheim give advice and stamps. x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Olav's Way St. Olavsleden Selånger to Trondheim: from the Baltic to the Atlantic in Olav's last footsteps Photo: Selångers kyrkoruin 04 by Hans Lindqvist, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Distance 564 km Days ~30 Start Selånger, Sundsvall (SE) Via Östersund · Åre · Stiklestad St. Olavsleden is one of the world's northernmost pilgrim paths, running 564 km from the Baltic coast of Sweden to the Atlantic fjords of Norway. It follows the way Olav himself took in 1030 , back from exile in Russia, across Sweden and over the mountains to his death at Stiklestad . It's the only St Olav Way that crosses a national border. Good to know Start: the ruined medieval church of Selånger , near Sundsvall, where Olav is said to have landed from the Baltic. Cycling: Åre to Trondheim (inner way) is about 252 km, 5 days, by bike. Getting there: fly or take the train to Sundsvall; the Mittbanan railway follows much of the route through Jämtland. St Olavsleden has its own official site, run by the Swedish and Norwegian partners: stolavsleden.com . Deep Dive History History. x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Olav's Way Stiklestad Where St Olav fell, 29 July 1030 Photo: Stiklestad kirke 21 by Lars Engerengen, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Where Verdal, Trøndelag Battle 29 July 1030 Church 12th century Olsok play Since 1954 On a farm slope above the Verdal valley, the course of Norwegian history turned. Here King Olav Haraldsson, back from exile, was killed in battle by his own people on 29 July 1030 , and here, within a year, began the cult that made him Norway's patron saint. Stiklestad is the most important stop on St. Olavsleden before Trondheim, and every summer it stages Norway's greatest open-air drama. x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Olav's Way Dovrefjell The mountain crossing: musk oxen, wild reindeer and the king's mountain lodges Photo: Dovre moskus IMG 9709 by Bjoertvedt, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Route Gudbrandsdalsleden High point ~1,300 m Open From ~10 June Wildlife Musk ox · reindeer Between Dombås and Oppdal, Gudbrandsdalsleden climbs onto Dovrefjell , a vast, treeless high plateau that was the hardest and most feared stage of the medieval pilgrimage. Its highest point on the trail is a little over 1,300 m . It's also one of the most beautiful: open sky, the peak of Snøhetta on the horizon, and herds of musk oxen and wild reindeer . Don't go too early. Until about 10 June the path over Dovrefjell is "technically closed": the footbridges over the rivers Hondyrju and Vesle Hondyrju are not yet in place, the rivers are full of ice water and can't be waded, and snow hides the waymarks. Two stretches cross wild reindeer calving areas. Take the train over the mountain if in doubt, and check the weather on yr.no: temperatures near 0 °C can occur in midsummer. Good to know Pilgrimssenter Dovrefjell gives advice on conditions; Budsjord pilgrim farm , the last stop before the climb, is a historic lodging. Musk oxen are large and dangerous if approached: keep at least 200 m away. Getting there: the Dovre railway stops at Dombås, Hjerkinn and Kongsvoll. d: Pilegrimsleden: the St Olav Ways to Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim

Pilgrims came over the mountains, along the fjords and from Sweden to the tomb of St Olav , the Viking king who brought Norway to Christ and died in battle at Stiklestad in 1030 . Since 1994 the old roads have been marked again, and today about 5,000 km of trails in Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland form Pilegrimsleden , the St Olav Ways, a Council of Europe Cultural Route. Good to know Nine routes, one goal. The official Norwegian network has nine ways: Gudbrandsdalsleden (Oslo–Trondheim, 643 km, about 32 days), St. Olavsleden (Selånger in Sweden–Trondheim, 564 km, about 30 days), Østerdalsleden (Trysil/Rena–Trondheim, 375 km, about 21 days), the coastal Kystpilegrimsleia (Egersund–Trondheim, by boat, bus and foot), Borgleden , Tunsbergleden , Valldalsleden , Romboleden and Nordleden . In 2026 the National Pilgrim Centre advises against walking Nordleden until its marking is improved. Season: the main season is 1 June to 1 September . Pilgrims set out from the Kilometre Zero stone outside the cathedral, after a blessing and the first stamp in the credential. Snow: walking over the pass is only advisable from about mid-June to September . Outside that season the path is under snow and avalanche-prone; take the bus or train via the road tunnel, or go with a mountain guide. The Hospice offers lodging and community meals all year (in summer also the Auberge de l'Hospice); book ahead. Visitors can join the canons' prayers; the church, the highest in Europe according to the Hospice, is free. d: Pavia, the Cisa Pass, Lucca, San Gimignano and Siena
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Via Francigena Lombardy, the Apennines and Tuscany Pavia, the Cisa Pass, Lucca, San Gimignano and Siena Photo: Torre Rognosa in San Gimignano Italy by Ввласенко, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Aosta to Siena about 600 km Apennines Cisa Pass, 1,041 m Most walked Lucca to Siena Relic Volto Santo, Lucca In Italy the road becomes busy with pilgrims. After the rice fields of the Po plain and the crossing of the Apennines, the Via Francigena enters Tuscany : walled towns, Romanesque churches, cypress-lined white roads and three of Italy's great pilgrim cities, Lucca , San Gimignano and Siena . Good to know Route: Aosta – Ivrea – Vercelli – Mortara – Pavia – the Po crossing (a ferry at Soprarivo, the Transitum Padi , booked in advance, or a road detour) – Piacenza – Fidenza – the Cisa Pass (1,041 m) – Pontremoli – Sarzana – Massa – Lucca – Altopascio – San Miniato – Gambassi – San Gimignano – Monteriggioni – Siena . Pilgrim hostels are frequent, many run by parishes and confraternities, often for a donation. Book ahead in May, June and September. Heat: in summer start at dawn. Water fountains are fewer in Tuscany than you might expect. Dress for churches: shoulders and knees covered. d: Canterbury to Rome, about 2,000 km on Archbishop Sigeric's road
x: Home › Pilgrimage Via Francigena Canterbury to Rome, about 2,000 km on Archbishop Sigeric's road Photo: Bosco cipressi Val d'Orcia Cassia by Unknown author, CC BY-SA 2.5 , via Wikimedia Commons "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD!'" (Psalm 122:1, ESV). For a thousand years Christians of the North walked to Rome to pray at the tombs of the Apostles Peter and Paul . Their road, the Via Francigena ("the road that comes from France"), runs about 2,000 km from Canterbury Cathedral , across the English Channel, through northern and eastern France, over the Alps at the Great St Bernard Pass and through Tuscany and Lazio to St Peter's Basilica . Its backbone is the diary of one man: Sigeric , Archbishop of Canterbury, who recorded his journey home from Rome in 990 . Good to know Distance and time: Canterbury to Rome is about 2,000 km, roughly 90–100 days on foot. Most pilgrims walk it in sections over several years. The most popular stretch by far is the Italian part, especially Lucca or Siena to Rome (about 3 weeks from Siena). Credential: carry the official pilgrim credential of the European Association of the Via Francigena Ways (EAVF) , sold by the Association, by Canterbury Cathedral and at points along the route. Stamp it at churches, hostels and town halls each day. The Jesus Trail is a waymarked 65 km footpath that follows the move of Jesus from his home town to the lake shore where his ministry began. It is the best way to feel the scale of Galilee: the distances Jesus walked, the hills, fields and springs of the parables. Good to know Stages (4 days): Nazareth – Cana (via Sepphoris), Cana – Kibbutz Lavi , Lavi – Moshav Arbel (via the Horns of Hattin and Nebi Shu'eib), Arbel – Capernaum (down the cliffs of Mount Arbel, through Magdala, Tabgha and the Mount of Beatitudes). Waymarks: orange-and-white blazes (some sections share the Israel National Trail). Season: March–May and October–November . Summer is very hot; carry 3 litres of water. Winter rain makes the Arbel descent slippery; it has fixed handholds and is steep. The first day is mostly through the urban edge of Nazareth; many start from Sepphoris or Cana. Accommodation: guesthouses in Nazareth's old city, B&Bs in Cana and Arbel, the kibbutz hotel at Lavi. The trail's official site lists them and sells guided and self-guided packages. x: Home › Pilgrimage The Holy Land Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth and Galilee, the land of the Gospels Photo: 2013-Aerial-Mount of Olives by Godot13, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Every Christian pilgrimage points back here. In Bethlehem the Word became flesh; in Nazareth he grew up; by the Sea of Galilee he called his disciples, taught and healed; in Jerusalem he died and rose again. "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14, ESV). Since at least the 4th century, when St Helena came and Egeria wrote her diary of the liturgy in Jerusalem, Christians have travelled to see and pray in the places of the Gospel. They call the land the Fifth Gospel . Check the situation before you book. As of 16 October 2026 the UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Gaza and to parts of the north and of the West Bank, and against all but essential travel to the rest of the West Bank except East Jerusalem, the Bethlehem governorate, Ramallah and Jericho; the US State Department rates Israel and the West Bank Level 3, "Reconsider travel". Group pilgrimages are running, and the Latin Patriarch and the Custos of the Holy Land have asked pilgrims to return, since local Christians depend on them. Read your government's advice the week you travel, go with a recognised pilgrimage organiser or local Christian guide, and expect last-minute changes, including at Holy Week. d: Our Lady of the Rosary and the three shepherd children, 1917
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Marian Shrines Fátima Our Lady of the Rosary and the three shepherd children, 1917 Photo: Fátima, Sanctuary of Our Lady of Fátima (6172325245) by Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium, CC BY 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Where Central Portugal, 125 km north of Lisbon Apparitions 13 May–13 October 1917 Seers Lúcia, Francisco, Jacinta Great days 12–13 May, 12–13 October "Pray the Rosary every day, in order to obtain peace for the world." In 1917, while the First World War raged, Our Lady appeared six times to three shepherd children in the Cova da Iria , a hollow of pasture near the village of Fátima. Today the Shrine of Our Lady of the Rosary of Fátima is one of the largest Marian sanctuaries in the world, and two of the children, Francisco and Jacinta Marto , are saints, the youngest non-martyrs ever canonized. Good to know The heart of the shrine is the small Chapel of the Apparitions ( Capelinha ), built on the spot of the apparitions; the Rosary is prayed there several times a day in different languages, broadcast online. Basilicas: the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary (1953), with the tombs of the three seers, and the large round Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity (2007). Candlelight procession every evening from spring to autumn after the evening Rosary, and the farewell procession on the 13th of the great months. Pilgrimage anniversaries: 12–13 May and 12–13 October , with hundreds of thousands present, and on the 13th of each month from June to Septem

d: The Immaculate Conception and St Bernadette, 1858
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Marian Shrines Lourdes The Immaculate Conception and St Bernadette, 1858 Photo: 00 1800 Rosenkranz-Basilika in Lourdes by W. Bulach, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Where Hautes-Pyrénées, France Apparitions 18 (February–July 1858) Recognised miracles 72 Season April–October "Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou", "I am the Immaculate Conception". With these words, in the dialect of the Pyrenees, the Lady of the grotto of Massabielle gave her name to Bernadette Soubirous , a poor, sickly, illiterate girl of fourteen. Since then Lourdes has become the great shrine of the sick , visited by millions each year. In September 2026 Pope Leo XIV came here on his apostolic journey to France. Good to know The Grotto is open day and night. Pilgrims touch the rock, light candles and drink from or wash at the fountains of the spring Bernadette uncovered. The baths ( piscines ): pilgrims can be immersed or washed in the spring water with the help of volunteers. Times vary by season; ask at the sanctuary. Daily processions (April–October): the Eucharistic procession with the blessing of the sick in the afternoon and the Marian torchlight procession at 21:00, singing the Lourdes Ave Maria . Churches: the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception (upper), the Rosary Basilica with its mosaics, the crypt , and the underground Basilica of St Pius X , which holds 25,000. d: Our Lady of Guadalupe and St Juan Diego, Mexico City, 1531
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Marian Shrines Guadalupe Our Lady of Guadalupe and St Juan Diego, Mexico City, 1531 Photo: Templo Expiatorio a Cristo Rey (Antigua Basílica de Guadalupe) - Ciudad de Méxic by Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Where Tepeyac, northern Mexico City Apparitions 9–12 December 1531 Feast 12 December Open daily 6:00–21:00 "¿No estoy yo aquí, que soy tu madre?", "Am I not here, I who am your mother?" These words of Our Lady to St Juan Diego , an Indigenous convert, at the hill of Tepeyac in December 1531 , are at the heart of the most visited Marian shrine in the world. Around 12 December alone, Mexico City counted some 13 million visitors in 2025. Pilgrims come to see the image of the Virgin on Juan Diego's cloak, the tilma , kept above the high altar of the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe . Good to know Hours: the Basilica is open daily 6:00–21:00 , with Masses at the high altar almost every hour from 6:00 to 20:00 (official timetable). The tilma hangs behind and above the altar; to see it close up, take the moving walkways that pass under it behind the sanctuary. The precinct ( Recinto Guadalupano ): the Old Basilica (1709, now the Expiatory Temple of Christ the King), the Capuchin church , the Chapel of the Well ( del Pocito ), and the steps and gardens up Tepeyac to the Capilla del Cerrito , built where the roses were gathered. 12 December: the feast begins at midnight with the Mañanitas , songs to the Virgin, followed by Masses

d: The Black Madonna of Jasna Góra, Queen of Poland
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Marian Shrines Częstochowa The Black Madonna of Jasna Góra, Queen of Poland Photo: Monastery at Jasna Góra Monastery, Częstochowa by Fotoomnia, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Where Częstochowa, southern Poland Since 1382 Feast 26 August Icon unveiled 6:00 daily On the "Bright Hill", Jasna Góra , above the city of Częstochowa, the Pauline Fathers have guarded since 1382 the icon of Our Lady of Częstochowa , the Black Madonna , with two scars on her cheek. It is the spiritual capital of Poland: through partitions, wars and Communism, Poles came here to pray for their nation, and still do in their hundreds of thousands, many on foot. Good to know The icon is shown in the Chapel of the Miraculous Image . It is unveiled at 6:00 every day to a fanfare, covered at 12:00 on weekdays (13:30 on Sundays and solemnities) and unveiled again at 13:30 on weekdays except Saturday (14:00 on Sundays). The Jasna Góra Appeal is sung before it every evening at 21:00 . Opening: the sanctuary gates are open about 5:00–21:45 ; the monastery entrance (through the Knights' Hall) 5:30–21:00 . Mass in the chapel runs from 6:00 to 18:30 (20:00 on Sundays). Also visit: the basilica , the treasury and museums, the bastions with the outdoor Way of the Cross, and the 106 m tower . August: the great walking pilgrimages arrive, above all around 15 August (Assumption) and 26 August (the feast of Our Lady of Częstochowa). x: Home › Pilgrimage Marian Shrines Fátima, Lourdes, Guadalupe and Częstochowa Photo: Torchlight Procession Rosary Square Lourdes by Laurence Goff, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons "For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed" (Luke 1:48, ESV). From the first centuries Christians have honoured Mary, the Mother of the Lord , and gone on pilgrimage to her shrines, not to put her in the place of Christ, but because she always points to him: "Do whatever he tells you" (John 2:5, ESV). Four shrines stand out for the crowds they draw and the place they hold in the life of the Church: Guadalupe in Mexico, Częstochowa in Poland, Lourdes in France and Fátima in Portugal. Good to know Apparitions and the Church: the Church never obliges Catholics to believe in a private revelation, even an approved one. It judges whether an apparition is "worthy of belief" and whether the devotion is sound; Lourdes, Fátima and Guadalupe have been approved by the local bishops and honoured by many popes. Częstochowa is an icon shrine, not an apparition. Great days: 12 December (Guadalupe), 11 February (Lourdes, first apparition; World Day of the Sick), 13 May and 13 October (Fátima), 26 August and 15 August (Częstochowa, with the great walking pilgrimages). What to expect: Mass in many languages, confession, the Rosary, candle processions, crowds on feast days and quiet in the off-season. Book rooms early for the big days. d: Melrose Abbey, the Eildon Hills and the Tweed
x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Cuthbert's Way Melrose to Harestanes Melrose Abbey, the Eildon Hills and the Tweed Photo: +1136 wurde Das Zisterienserkloster Melrose gegründet. 03 by Holger Uwe Schmitt, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Distance 24 km (15 miles) Time 6–8 hours Start Melrose Abbey gates Climb Eildon Hills The Way starts at the gates of Melrose Abbey , the most beautiful ruin in the Borders, and climbs at once over the three summits of the Eildon Hills , from which, on a clear day, you can see the whole road ahead to the Cheviots. Good to know Route: Melrose – Eildon Hills – Bowden – Newtown St Boswells – along the Tweed past Dryburgh Abbey (across the river) – St Boswells – the Roman road of Dere Street – Harestanes visitor centre near Ancrum. Melrose Abbey is cared for by Historic Environment Scotland; check opening times and tickets on its site. The tradition is that the heart of Robert the Bruce is buried here. Old Melrose , the site of Cuthbert's monastery, is on a loop of the Tweed 3 km east of the town, on private land; it can be seen from the riverside path. Getting there: the Borders Railway from Edinburgh to Tweedbank , 3 km from Melrose. Deep Dive Old Melrose and Cuthbert's monastery History. Cuthbert's Melrose was not the abbey in the town but Mailros , a monastery founded by St Aidan's monks around 640 on a promontory in a loop of the Tweed, now Old Melrose . x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Cuthbert's Way Harestanes to Kirk Yetholm The Teviot, Cessford Castle and Wideopen Hill Photo: Cessford Castle ruins by Weirdcrank, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Distance 28 km (17.5 miles) Time 6–7 hours Highest point Wideopen Hill, 400 m Halfway Melrose–Holy Island The longest day crosses rich farmland and then climbs into the hills. At the top of Wideopen Hill , at 400 m the highest point of the Way, you are exactly halfway from Melrose to Holy Island, and can look back to the Eildons and forward to the Cheviots. Good to know Route: Harestanes – Monteviot suspension bridge over the Teviot – Jedfoot (back on Dere Street) – woodland and farm tracks – Cessford Castle – Morebattle (shop, inn) – Grubbit Law – Wideopen Hill – Town Yetholm – Kirk Yetholm . Jedburgh Abbey is a 5 km detour from Jedfoot and worth it if you have a spare half day. Kirk Yetholm is also the northern end of the Pennine Way ; the Border Hotel has welcomed walkers from both trails for decades. Book beds early. Break the day at Morebattle if 28 km is too far. Deep Dive A border country History. For centuries this was the land of the Border Reivers , raiding families on both sides of the frontier. Cessford Castle , a massive L-plan tower house of the 15th century, was the stronghold of the Kers , wardens of the Middle March; it was besieged by the English in 1523 and is now a roofless shell beside the path. x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Cuthbert's Way The Cheviots to the coast Kirk Yetholm to Wooler and Fenwick, past St Cuthbert's Cave Photo: College Valley panorama from the north-east slope of Great Hetha - geograph.org. by Andrew Curtis, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Kirk Yetholm–Wooler 19 km Wooler–Fenwick 19 km Border crossed above Halterburn Cave St Cuthbert's Cave "They shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint" (Isaiah 40:31, ESV). On the third day the Way crosses the border into England and the Northumberland National Park , among Iron Age hillforts, then descends to the market town of Wooler . On the fourth it crosses the moors to the sandstone overhang of St Cuthbert's Cave , and from the Kyloe Hills above it walkers see Holy Island for the first time. Good to know Kirk Yetholm – Wooler (19 km, 6–7 hours): shared at first with the Pennine Way; over the border near Eccles Cairn; down to Hethpool at the mouth of the College Valley ; under Yeavering Bell (361 m), Northumberland's largest hillfort; into Wooler. Wooler – Fenwick (19 km, about 4 hours): Weetwood Moor (prehistoric rock art nearby), the 16th-century Weetwood Bridge over the Till, the Roman Devil's Causeway , then woods to St Cuthbert's Cave (National Trust). d: The Pilgrims' Way over the sands, the priory and the Farne Islands
x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Cuthbert's Way Holy Island (Lindisfarne) The Pilgrims' Way over the sands, the priory and the Farne Islands Photo: Lindisfarne Castle reflection - geograph.org.uk - 8163230 by Walter Baxter, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Fenwick–Holy Island 10 km Sands crossing about 5 km, marked by poles Founded 635, by St Aidan Feast St Cuthbert, 20 March The last stage ends on the sands. At low tide, pilgrims leave their boots on the shore and walk barefoot over the wet flats, following the line of tall posts of the Pilgrims' Way , toward the island where St Aidan founded his monastery in 635 and from which the Gospel spread across the North of England. Good to know Safe crossing times for the road causeway are published by Northumberland County Council for every day of the year. Never start when the tide is rising. The sands route is shorter in time: aim to finish before the mid-point of the safe period, in daylight; refuge boxes on posts are for emergencies. Every year cars and walkers are caught by the tide. Lindisfarne Priory (English Heritage) has the ruins of the 12th-century Benedictine priory built in Cuthbert's memory, and a museum. St Mary's Church , the parish church beside the priory, stands on the probable site of Aidan's first church; pilgrim groups use it and the island's retreat houses. d: The shrine of St Cuthbert and the tomb of St Bede
x: Home › Pilgrimage › St Cuthbert's Way Durham Cathedral The shrine of St Cuthbert and the tomb of St Bede Photo: Durham Cathedral from the river - geograph.org.uk - 5351542 by Malcolm Neal, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Begun 1093 Open Mon–Sat 8:00–18:00, Sun 8:00–17:00 Entry free (£5 donation suggested) UNESCO since 1986 Since 995 St Cuthbert has rested in Durham , on a rocky peninsula in a loop of the River Wear. Around his tomb the Normans built from 1093 one of the greatest Romanesque churches in Europe. Many walkers of St Cuthbert's Way finish here, by train or on foot along the coastal routes, to pray at his shrine. Good to know Hours: the cathedral is open Monday–Saturday 8:00–18:00 (all areas 9:30–16:30) and Sunday 8:00–17:00 (all areas 12:30–15:00). Entry is free ; a £5 donation is suggested. Parts can be closed for services and events; check the calendar. The Shrine of St Cuthbert is in the Feretory behind the high altar, a simple slab inscribed Cuthbertus . The Venerable Bede lies in the Galilee Chapel at the west end. Cuthbert Centre for Pilgrimage and Prayer: newly opened in the Chapel of the Holy Cross, it welcomes pilgrims and groups with hospitality and resources. The Treasures: Cuthbert's oak coffin , his pectoral cross , embroidered stole and other relics found in the tomb are shown in the cathedral museum. d: Melrose to Holy Island, 100 km from Scotland to England
x: Home › Pilgrimage St Cuthbert's Way Melrose to Holy Island, 100 km from Scotland to England Photo: Lindisfarne Priory ruins - geograph.org.uk - 7550660 by Andy Stephenson, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons St Cuthbert's Way joins the two places that framed the life of the North's best-loved saint: Melrose , where the young shepherd Cuthbert became a monk in 651 , and Holy Island , Lindisfarne , where he was prior and bishop and where he was first buried. The 100 km route (62.5 miles), opened in 1996 , crosses the Scottish Borders and Northumberland and ends with an unforgettable walk over the tidal sands, following the poles of the old Pilgrims' Way . Good to know Stages (official): Melrose – Harestanes 24 km; Harestanes – Kirk Yetholm 28 km; Kirk Yetholm – Wooler 19 km; Wooler – Fenwick 19 km; Fenwick – Holy Island 10 km. Most walkers take 4–6 days . The highest point is Wideopen Hill (400 m), halfway. Tides decide the last day. Holy Island is cut off twice a day. Check the Northumberland County Council safe crossing times before you set out from Fenwick, and add 30 minutes for weather. The walking route over the sands has its own rule: cross only in daylight, never on a rising tide, and finish before the mid-point of the safe period. Waymarks: a Celtic cross symbol, with the Way's name. The route is one of Scotland's Great Trails . Certificate: the official completion certificate is sent to walkers who return the questionnaire at the back of the official guidebook. Seaso

d: The mountain of the stigmata, where the way begins
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Assisi and the Way of St Francis La Verna The mountain of the stigmata, where the way begins Photo: Chiusi della verna, santuario francescano, chiesa maggiore, esterno 01 by Sailko, CC BY 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Height 1,128 m Given to Francis 1213 Stigmata September 1224 Feast of the Stigmata 17 September The sanctuary of La Verna stands on a crag of beech and fir above the Casentino valley. Here, in September 1224, two years before his death, Francis received the wounds of Christ. For most pilgrims it is the starting point of the Via di Francesco; others walk here first from Florence in about five days. Good to know The Franciscan friars run the sanctuary and a guesthouse; pilgrims can sleep there. The friars process every afternoon from the basilica to the Chapel of the Stigmata , a custom kept without a break for centuries. See the Chiesa Maggiore with the great glazed terracottas of Andrea della Robbia , the Chapel of the Stigmata , the Sasso Spicco (the overhanging rock where Francis prayed) and the bed of stone in the cave. From La Verna, the first stage drops to Pieve Santo Stefano and the second to Sansepolcro . Deep Dive The mountain History. Count Orlando of Chiusi gave the mountain to Francis in 1213 as a place of solitude. Francis came there many times to keep the "Lent of St Michael" (15 August – 29 September). d: The northern way through the upper Tiber valley and the Umbrian hills
x: Home › Pilgrimage › Assisi and the Way of St Francis Sansepolcro to Gubbio and Assisi The northern way through the upper Tiber valley and the Umbrian hills Photo: Palazzo dei Consoli,Gubbio by Livioandronico2013, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Sansepolcro – Assisi about 140 km Stages 7 Longest stage Città di Castello – Pietralunga, 31 km Highlight Gubbio, the wolf legend After La Verna the way leaves Tuscany for Umbria. It follows the young Tiber past Sansepolcro and Città di Castello , climbs through lonely woods to Pietralunga and reaches Gubbio , the stone town of the wolf story, before the last long days to Assisi. Good to know Stages: Sansepolcro – Citerna 11.7 km; Citerna – Città di Castello 19.4 km; Città di Castello – Pietralunga 31 km; Pietralunga – Gubbio 26 km; Gubbio – San Pietro in Vigneto 16.3 km; San Pietro in Vigneto – Valfabbrica 21.9 km; Valfabbrica – Assisi 13.4 km. Near Sansepolcro, the hermitage of Montecasale is a short detour where Francis stayed. In Gubbio , the little church of Santa Maria della Vittoria ( La Vittorina ) marks where Francis is said to have met the wolf; the Corsa dei Ceri (15 May) honours St Ubaldo, the town's bishop and patron. The last stage enters Assisi on the slope beneath the Basilica, a famous first sight. Deep Dive Gubbio and Francis History. x: Home › Pilgrimage › Assisi and the Way of St Francis Assisi The Basilica of St Francis, St Clare, San Damiano, the Portiuncula and the Carceri Photo: Assisi San Francesco BW 2 by Berthold Werner, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Basilica begun 1228 Tomb found 1818 UNESCO 2000 Feast St Francis, 4 October Assisi is where the way gathers. Every place in this small pink-stone town on Monte Subasio speaks of Francis and Clare: his tomb, her basilica, the chapel where Christ spoke from the cross, the little church where he died, and the caves where the brothers prayed. Assisi's Franciscan sites have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2000 . Good to know Basilica of St Francis: Upper Church with Giotto's cycle of the life of Francis; Lower Church with frescoes by Cimabue , Simone Martini and Pietro Lorenzetti ; the tomb in the crypt. The last stretch of the Via di Francesco retraces that journey through the Sabine hills and the Tiber valley to the Lateran, the Pope's cathedral, and on to St Peter's. Good to know From the Rieti valley the way runs by Poggio San Lorenzo , Ponticelli , Monterotondo and Monte Sacro into the city, in about 5 to 6 days. In Rome, St John Lateran recalls the approval of the Rule. San Francesco a Ripa in Trastevere keeps the cell where Francis stayed. Francis and his first companions brought a short rule made of Gospel sayings to Innocent III . With the help of Bishop Guido of Assisi and Cardinal John of St Paul, the Pope gave verbal approval and permission to preach penance. d: Via di Francesco, from La Verna through Gubbio and Assisi to the Rieti valley and Rome
x: Home › Pilgrimage Assisi and the Way of St Francis Via di Francesco, from La Verna through Gubbio and Assisi to the Rieti valley and Rome Photo: Rear NW Basilica Francesco Assisi Sep23 A7C 07913 by Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons The Way of St Francis ( Via di Francesco ) follows the hill paths of Tuscany, Umbria and Lazio that Francis of Assisi (1181/82–1226) walked as a preacher and a beggar. It joins the places of his life: La Verna , where he received the stigmata; Gubbio , where legend says he tamed the wolf; Assisi , his home town and the place of his tomb; the Rieti valley , where he made the first Christmas crib at Greccio ; and Rome , where Pope Innocent III approved his way of life. The year 2026 is the 800th anniversary of his death (3–4 October 1226). Good to know Two halves. The northern way runs La Verna – Assisi (about 8 to 10 days); the southern way runs Assisi – Rieti valley (about 8 days) and on to Rome (another 5 to 6). The whole way from La Verna to Rome is roughly 500 km. Waymarks: the yellow Tau and yellow-and-blue signs. Credential: order the official pilgrim credential from the Via di Francesco at least 3 weeks ahead, or 2 months if it must be posted outside Italy. Testimonium: for at least 100 km on foot or 200 km by bike , collected at the Statio Peregrinorum , Piazza Inferiore di San Francesco 2, Assisi (10:00–12:30 and 15:00–17:30; +39 075 819001). Lived 1st century BC – 1st century AD, Nazareth Feast days 1 Jan, 25 Mar, 31 May, 15 Aug, 8 Dec (and more) Recognised Pre-Congregation (biblical) Place Nazareth, Bethlehem, Jerusalem, Ephesus Her story Mary of Nazareth was a young Jewish woman betrothed to Joseph, a carpenter of David's line, when the angel Gabriel announced that she would conceive a son by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:26-38). Her answer, "be it unto me according to thy word", is remembered in every Angelus. She visited her cousin Elizabeth and sang the **Magnificat**, gave birth in Bethlehem, presented Jesus in the Temple, searched for him when he was twelve, prompted his first sign at **Cana** ("Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it", John 2:5), stood at the **Cross**, and prayed with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). Tradition: The 2nd-century Protoevangelium of James names her parents Joachim and Anne. Ancient tradition places her last years either in Jerusalem or at Ephesus with St John, to whom Jesus entrusted her from the Cross. What the Church teaches Mother of God ( Theotokos ) , defined at the Council of Ephesus (431): because Jesus is one divine Person, his mother is truly the Mother of God. x: Home › Saints St Michael the Archangel Prince of the heavenly host The Archangel Michael Defeating Satan (1636) , Guido Reni · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived An angel: not a human life Feast day 29 September (Michaelmas) Recognised Scripture & ancient tradition Who he is Michael (Hebrew Mi-ka-El , "Who is like God?") appears in Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1 as a great prince who protects God's people, in Jude 9 disputing with the devil, and in Revelation 12:7–9 leading the angels against the dragon. Christians, Jews and Muslims all honour him. Path to sainthood Michael is not a canonised human but one of the three archangels named in the Catholic canon (with Gabriel and Raphael), venerated since the earliest centuries. Since the 1969 calendar reform the three share the feast of 29 September . Patronages Soldiers, police officers, paramedics, the sick, and a good death. Trivia Pope Leo XIII added the short Prayer to St Michael in 1886 to the prayers he had ordered said after Low Mass in 1884. The famous story that he wrote it after a vision of Satan during Mass first appeared in the 1930s, with conflicting details and no contemporary evidence, so treat it as legend. Michaelmas was one of the four "quarter days" when rents were due in England, and it gave its name to Oxford and Cambridge's autumn Michaelmas term . d: Fisherman, apostle, first bishop of Rome
x: Home › Saints St Peter Fisherman, apostle, first bishop of Rome Crucifixion of Saint Peter (1600) , Caravaggio · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. AD 64–67, Rome Feast day 29 June (with St Paul) Recognised Pre-Congregation (apostle) His story Simon, a fisherman from Bethsaida working at Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee, was called by Jesus with his brother Andrew (Mark 1:16–18). Jesus renamed him Kephas/Petros , "Rock" (Matthew 16:18). He denied Jesus three times, was restored after the Resurrection (John 21), led the early Jerusalem church, and according to tradition died a martyr in Rome under Nero. Path to sainthood An apostle, venerated from the beginning. No formal canonisation (pre-Congregation). Catholic tradition regards him as the first pope. Patronages Fishermen, net makers, popes, and locksmiths (the keys of the kingdom). Trivia Early tradition (recorded by Origen, via Eusebius) says he asked to be crucified upside down , feeling unworthy to die as Jesus did. Excavations under St Peter's Basilica in the 1940s–60s found a 1st-century tomb area. On 26 June 1968 Pope Paul VI announced that bones found there had been identified "in a way we can consider convincing" as Peter's, based largely on Margherita Guarducci's work. He stopped short of certainty, and scholars still debate it. Peter's in-law appears in the Gospels: Jesus healed his mother-in-law (Mark 1:30), so Peter was married. d: Apostle to the Gentiles

AD 5 – c. 64/67 Feast day 29 June; Conversion: 25 January Recognised Pre-Congregation (apostle) His story Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee and Roman citizen, persecuted the first Christians until the risen Christ stopped him on the road to Damascus (Acts 9). He became the great missionary of the early Church, travelling thousands of miles through Asia Minor and Greece, founding churches and writing letters that make up much of the New Testament. Tradition says he was beheaded in Rome under Nero. Path to sainthood Venerated as an apostle from the beginning (pre-Congregation). His tomb is honoured at the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls. Patronages Missionaries, writers, journalists, theologians, and tentmakers. Trivia He made a living as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name. Scholars agree almost universally that seven are his own; authorship of the others is debated. On 28 June 2009 Pope Benedict XVI announced that bone fragments from the sarcophagus under St Paul Outside the Walls had been carbon-dated to the 1st or 2nd century, which he said "seems to confirm" the tradition that they are Paul's. She followed him and supported his ministry, stood at the cross, and was the first witness of the Resurrection : Jesus sent her to tell the disciples (John 20:11–18). Path to sainthood Venerated since the early Church (pre-Congregation). By a decree of 3 June 2016 , issued at Pope Francis 's wish by the Congregation for Divine Worship, her memorial was raised to a full feast , the same rank as the apostles. The decree calls her the "apostle of the apostles", a title it takes from St Thomas Aquinas. Patronages Converts, penitents, perfumers, hairdressers, and contemplatives. Trivia In his Homily 33 of 591, Pope Gregory the Great merged her with the unnamed "sinful woman" of Luke 7, creating the long-lived but unbiblical image of her as a repentant prostitute. The 1969 calendar reform separated them. A legend says she showed the Emperor Tiberius an egg that turned red, a story linked to the custom of red Easter eggs ⚠ (legend). French tradition places her last years in a cave at La Sainte-Baume in Provence. d: Bishop, Doctor of the Church, author of the Confessions

A brilliant teacher of rhetoric, he wandered through Manichaeism and a worldly life before converting in Milan in 386 under St Ambrose. He became Bishop of Hippo, wrote Confessions and The City of God , and shaped Western theology more than almost anyone after Paul. Path to sainthood Venerated immediately after his death (pre-Congregation). Named one of the four original Doctors of the Church (with Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory) by Pope Boniface VIII in 1298 . Patronages Theologians, printers, brewers, and those struggling with sin. Trivia His famous youthful prayer: "Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet" ( Confessions VIII). He converted after hearing a child chant "Tolle, lege" ("Take up and read"). He opened Paul's letters at Romans 13:13–14. He died in 430 while the Vandals besieged Hippo . x: Home › Saints St Thomas Aquinas The Angelic Doctor Saint Thomas Aquinas (1476) , Carlo Crivelli · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 1225 – 7 March 1274 Feast day 28 January Recognised Canonised 18 July 1323, Pope John XXII His story Born to a noble family at Roccasecca near Aquino, Italy, he joined the new, poor Dominican order against his family's wishes. He studied under Albert the Great and taught in Paris and Italy. His Summa Theologiae united faith and Aristotle's philosophy and remains a cornerstone of Catholic theology. Path to sainthood Canonised on 18 July 1323 by Pope John XXII in Avignon. Declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Pius V in 1567 . Patronages Students, universities, Catholic schools, theologians, and pencil makers. Trivia His family kidnapped him and held him for about a year to stop him becoming a Dominican. Fellow students called the quiet, heavy-set Thomas "the Dumb Ox" . Albert the Great replied that this ox would one day "bellow so loud his bellowing will fill the world." After an experience during Mass in December 1273 he stopped writing, saying everything he had written seemed "like straw". The Summa was left unfinished. d: Apostle of Ireland
x: Home › Saints St Patrick Apostle of Ireland St Patrick window, St Patrick's Church, Junction City, Ohio , photo by Nheyob · CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived 5th century (exact dates uncertain ⚠) Feast day 17 March Recognised Pre-Congregation His story Born in Roman Britain to a Christian family, Patrick was captured by Irish raiders at about 16 and spent six years herding animals in Ireland, where he turned to prayer. He escaped and went home, then came back as a bishop to evangelise the Irish. His own Confessio survives, one of the earliest documents of Irish history. Path to sainthood Venerated by popular acclaim long before the formal process existed (pre-Congregation). Patronages Ireland, Nigeria, engineers, and the Archdiocese of New York. Trivia He wasn't Irish : he was a Roman Briton. There have been no snakes in Ireland since the last Ice Age, so the snake legend is symbolic. d: Little poor man of Assisi

He rebuilt ruined churches, founded the Franciscan friars, helped St Clare found the Poor Clares, and preached peace, even crossing Crusader lines in 1219 to meet Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt. Path to sainthood Canonised less than two years after his death, on 16 July 1228 , by Pope Gregory IX , a personal friend. Pius XII named him a patron of Italy in 1939, and John Paul II named him patron of ecology in 1979. Patronages Italy, animals, ecology, and merchants. Trivia He set up the first live nativity scene at Greccio in 1223. In 1224 he received the stigmata on Mount La Verna, the first widely recorded case in history. His Canticle of the Sun is one of the earliest poems written in Italian. Pope Francis (elected 2013) was the first pope to take his name. She succeeded, and Charles was crowned at Reims. She was captured, tried for heresy by a pro-English church court, and burned at the stake in Rouen at about 19 . Path to sainthood A retrial in 1456 declared her innocent. She was beatified on 18 April 1909 by Pope Pius X and canonised on 16 May 1920 by Pope Benedict XV . Patronages France (secondary patron, proclaimed by Pius XI on 2 March 1922), soldiers, and women in military service. Trivia Among the charges against her was wearing men's clothing . St Michael was one of her voices, which ties her to St Michael's Line and Mont-Saint-Michel, which never fell to the English. She could not read or write, but her signature ("Jehanne") survives on letters she dictated. d: Reformer of Carmel, mystic, Doctor of the Church
x: Home › Saints St Teresa of Ávila Reformer of Carmel, mystic, Doctor of the Church Saint Teresa of Ávila Interceding for Souls in Purgatory , Peter Paul Rubens · CC0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived 28 March 1515 – 4 October 1582 Feast day 15 October Recognised Canonised 12 March 1622 (Gregory XV); Doctor 1970 Her story A lively Spanish noblewoman who entered the Carmelite convent in Ávila. After years of lukewarm prayer, a deep conversion in her late thirties led her to found the reformed Discalced Carmelites with St John of the Cross. Her books The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection are classics of prayer. Path to sainthood Beatified in 1614 by Pope Paul V . Canonised on 12 March 1622 by Pope Gregory XV , on the same day as Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Isidore the Farmer and Philip Neri. In 1970 Pope Paul VI made her the first woman Doctor of the Church . Patronages Spain, writers, people in religious life, and headache sufferers. Trivia She died on the night Catholic countries switched to the Gregorian calendar : the day after 4 October 1582 was 15 October, which is why her feast is the 15th. A much-loved story has her telling God after a mishap on the road, "If this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few!" ⚠ It isn't in her own writings or in the first biography; the earliest known version is from 1912, so it is probably legend. d: The Little Flower
x: Home › Saints St Thérèse of Lisieux The Little Flower Thérèse of Lisieux, photograph (c. 1888) , unknown photographer · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 2 January 1873 – 30 September 1897 Feast day 1 October Recognised Canonised 17 May 1925 (Pius XI); Doctor 1997 Her story The youngest daughter of a devout family in Normandy, Thérèse entered the Carmel of Lisieux at just 15 and died of tuberculosis at 24 . Her autobiography, Story of a Soul , describing her "Little Way" of doing small things with great love, became one of the most-read spiritual books of the 20th century. Path to sainthood Beatified on 29 April 1923 and canonised on 17 May 1925 , both by Pope Pius XI . John Paul II declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1997 . Patronages Missions (named by Pius XI on 14 December 1927, alongside St Francis Xavier, though she never left her convent), florists, France (secondary patron), and people with tuberculosis. Trivia At 14 she broke protocol during a papal audience and asked Pope Leo XIII in person for permission to enter Carmel early. Her parents, Louis and Zélie Martin , were canonised together by Pope Francis on 18 October 2015 , the first married couple canonised in the same ceremony. She promised to "spend my heaven doing good on earth" and to let fall "a shower of roses". Roses are her symbol.
