Her private letters, published in 2007 as Come Be My Light , revealed that she felt spiritual darkness for nearly 50 years while she kept smiling and serving. d: Pope from 1978 to 2005
x: Home › Saints St John Paul II Pope from 1978 to 2005 John Paul II in Katowice, Poland (1983) , photo by Bernard Gotfryd · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 18 May 1920 – 2 April 2005 Feast day 22 October Recognised Beatified 1 May 2011 (Benedict XVI); canonised 27 April 2014 (Francis) His story Karol Wojtyła, born in Wadowice, Poland, lost his mother, brother and father by age 20. He worked in a quarry and acted in underground theatre during the Nazi occupation while secretly studying for the priesthood. Elected pope in 1978, the first non-Italian pope in 455 years, he made 104 international journeys to 129 countries and helped inspire the peaceful end of communism in Eastern Europe. Path to sainthood Crowds shouted "Santo subito!" ("Sainthood now!") at his funeral. Pope Benedict XVI waived the usual five-year wait. He was beatified on 1 May 2011 by Benedict XVI , after the healing of Sr Marie Simon-Pierre from Parkinson's disease. He was canonised on 27 April 2014 by Pope Francis , after the healing of Floribeth Mora Díaz of Costa Rica (a brain aneurysm), on the same day as St John XXIII . Trivia He survived being shot in St Peter's Square on 13 May 1981 , the feast of Our Lady of Fátima, and later visited his attacker in prison to forgive him. d: Deacon and first Christian martyr
x: Home › Saints St Stephen Deacon and first Christian martyr The Stoning of Saint Stephen (1625) , Rembrandt · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. AD 34–36, Jerusalem Feast day 26 December Recognised Pre-Congregation (biblical) His story Stephen was one of the seven men chosen by the apostles to serve the Greek-speaking widows of the Jerusalem church (Acts 6:1–6), the first "deacons". Acts calls him "full of grace and power". Accused of speaking against the Temple and the Law, he gave a long speech before the Sanhedrin retelling Israel's history (Acts 7), saw "the heavens opened", and was dragged out of the city and stoned. He died praying, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." A young man named Saul , later the apostle Paul, guarded the cloaks of the men who stoned him (Acts 7:58). Path to sainthood Venerated from the earliest days of the Church as the protomartyr (first martyr). No formal canonisation (pre-Congregation). Patronages Deacons, stonemasons, headaches. Trivia His feast falls on 26 December , the day after Christmas; the carol Good King Wenceslas is set "on the Feast of Stephen". According to a 5th-century account, a priest named Lucian reported finding Stephen's relics in 415 after a dream; much of this story is tradition. His name in Greek, Stephanos , means "crown", a play on words early writers loved: the first martyr received the first crown. Sources Benedict XVI, General Audience "Stephen, the Protomartyr" (10 Jan 2007), vatican.va Vatican N

AD 60 (tradition), Patras Feast day 30 November Recognised Pre-Congregation (apostle) His story Andrew was a fisherman from Bethsaida and Simon Peter's brother. John's Gospel says he was first a disciple of John the Baptist, followed Jesus, and then brought his brother to him: "We have found the Messiah" (John 1:40–42). The Eastern Church calls him the Protoklētos , the "First-called". He appears at the feeding of the five thousand, pointing out the boy with five loaves and two fish (John 6:8–9). AD 100 (tradition), Ephesus Feast day 27 December Recognised Pre-Congregation (apostle) His story John and his brother James, fishermen and sons of Zebedee, left their nets to follow Jesus (Mark 1:19–20); Jesus nicknamed them Boanerges , "sons of thunder". With Peter and James he witnessed the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane. Christian tradition identifies him with the "disciple whom Jesus loved", to whom Jesus entrusted his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). Tradition also attributes to him the fourth Gospel, three letters and Revelation (written on the island of Patmos); modern scholars debate these attributions. According to Irenaeus, he lived to old age at Ephesus. Path to sainthood An apostle, venerated from the beginning. No formal canonisation (pre-Congregation). A legend says he was handed a poisoned cup and blessed it, and the poison left as a serpent; that's why he is often painted holding a chalice with a snake. His symbol among the four evangelists is the eagle , because his Gospel soars into theology from its first line, "In the beginning was the Word". d: Bishop of Myra, the original Santa Claus
x: Home › Saints St Nicholas Bishop of Myra, the original Santa Claus The Sick Cured at the Tomb of Saint Nicholas (1425) , Gentile da Fabriano · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. AD 343 (traditional), Myra Feast day 6 December Recognised Pre-Congregation His story Nicholas was bishop of Myra in Lycia (in today's Turkey) in the 4th century. Reliable historical details are few; most of what is told about him comes from later lives and legends. The best-loved story says he secretly threw bags of gold through a poor man's window at night so that his three daughters would have dowries and not be sold into slavery. Other stories tell of him saving sailors in a storm, rescuing innocent men from execution, and (in a later legend) restoring three murdered boys to life. Path to sainthood Venerated since the early centuries, especially in the East. No formal canonisation (pre-Congregation). Patronages Children, sailors, Russia, Greece, pawnbrokers, the city of Bari. Trivia In 1087 sailors from Bari carried his relics from Myra to Italy, where they still rest in the Basilica of San Nicola. The Dutch Sinterklaas , brought to New York, grew into Santa Claus . AD 303, Lydda (Palestine) Feast day 23 April Recognised Pre-Congregation His story George was a soldier who, according to early tradition, was martyred at Lydda (modern Lod, Israel) around 303, during the persecution under Diocletian. His cult spread widely and early, but the details of his life are uncertain; already in 494 a list attributed to Pope Gelasius placed him among saints "whose names are justly reverenced among men, but whose acts are known only to God". The famous dragon story appears only centuries later and was popularised by the 13th-century Golden Legend : George kills a dragon that terrorises a town and rescues a princess, and the town is baptised. Trivia The red cross on a white field of England's flag is St George's cross. In Catalonia, 23 April (Sant Jordi) is a day for giving roses and books. The dragon legend is medieval; the historical George, if we knew more, would have been a Roman soldier, not a knight. d: Father of Western monasticism, patron of Europe
x: Home › Saints St Benedict Father of Western monasticism, patron of Europe Saint Benedict (c. 1495–98) , Pietro Perugino · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 480–547 (traditional), Nursia–Monte Cassino Feast day 11 July Recognised Pre-Congregation His story Almost all we know of Benedict comes from Book II of the Dialogues of Pope Gregory the Great , written about 50 years after his death. Born at Nursia (Norcia) in Umbria, he left his studies in Rome to live as a hermit in a cave at Subiaco, attracted followers, founded small monasteries and around 529 established the abbey of Monte Cassino . There he wrote his Rule , a short, practical and moderate guide to community life summed up later in the phrase ora et labora , "pray and work". His twin sister, St Scholastica, led a community of women nearby. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint. Pope Paul VI proclaimed him Patron of Europe in 1964 with the apostolic letter Pacis Nuntius . Patronages Europe, monks, farmers, against poison. Trivia Gregory tells how monks tried to poison his wine and the cup shattered when he blessed it, which is why the St Benedict medal is used against evil. Monte Cassino was destroyed and rebuilt several times, last after the Allied bombing of 1944. The Rule of St Benedict is still followed by thousands of Benedictine, Cistercian and Trappist monks and nuns. d: Apostle and Evangelist, the tax collector who followed
x: Home › Saints St Matthew Apostle and Evangelist, the tax collector who followed Artistic illustration in a Renaissance fresco style, created for The Daily Word; not a historical likeness. Matthew writing his Gospel, guided by an angel (his symbol). Lived 1st century, Capernaum Feast day 21 September Recognised Pre-Congregation (apostle) Place Capernaum; Salerno, Italy His story Matthew (also called **Levi**) was a tax collector at Capernaum, working for Herod Antipas: a man most of his neighbours would have regarded as a collaborator. Jesus saw him at the tax booth and said "Follow me", "and he arose, and followed him" (Matthew 9:9). He then threw a dinner for Jesus with other tax collectors and sinners, prompting the line "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Tradition: Papias of Hierapolis (early 2nd century) says Matthew "compiled the sayings in the Hebrew language", and the Church has always attached his name to the first Gospel. Later traditions send him to preach in Ethiopia or Persia and tell of his martyrdom; they differ. His Gospel in the Church year Matthew is the Gospel of Lectionary Year A , the most quoted in the liturgy: the Sermon on the Mount, the Lord's Prayer as Christians pray it, the Magi, and the Great Commission. Several Daily Word verses so far ( Matthew 6:9–13 , 16:18 , 4:17 ) come from it. His symbol is a winged man or angel , because his Gospel begins with Jesus' human genealogy. Patronages Accountants, bankers, tax collector

d: Founder of the Order of Preachers
x: Home › Saints St Dominic Founder of the Order of Preachers Saint Dominic in Prayer (c. 1605) , El Greco · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 1170–1221, Caleruega–Bologna Feast day 8 August Recognised Canonised 1234 (Gregory IX) His story Dominic de Guzmán was a Castilian priest, a canon of Osma, who while travelling through southern France met the Cathar movement and decided that the Church needed well-educated, poor, itinerant preachers to answer it. He gathered companions in Toulouse, and in 1216 Pope Honorius III approved the Order of Preachers (the Dominicans). He sent his friars to the great university cities, Paris and Bologna, making study central to the order. He died at Bologna in 1221. Path to sainthood Canonised by Pope Gregory IX in 1234 , just 13 years after his death. Patronages Astronomers, the Dominican Republic. Trivia A popular tradition says the Virgin Mary gave Dominic the rosary ; historians see the rosary developing gradually, and the story spread mainly from the 15th century. Famous Dominicans include Thomas Aquinas , Catherine of Siena (a lay Dominican) and Fra Angelico. Dominicans still use the initials O.P. ( Ordo Praedicatorum ) after their names. Luke painting the Madonna (a medieval legend), with the winged ox, his symbol. Lived 1st century, Antioch (tradition) Feast day 18 October Recognised Pre-Congregation (evangelist) Place Antioch; Padua, Italy His story Luke wrote the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, together about a quarter of the New Testament. St Paul calls him "Luke, the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14) and his loyal companion ("Only Luke is with me", 2 Timothy 4:11). The "we" passages of Acts (16:10 onward) suggest he travelled with Paul. He was probably a Gentile; he opens his Gospel like a Greek historian, having "traced the course of all things accurately from the first" (Luke 1:3). Tradition: Early writers say he came from Antioch and died at 84 in Boeotia, Greece. A medieval legend says he painted the first icon of the Virgin Mary; several famous icons, such as the Salus Populi Romani in Santa Maria Maggiore, were attributed to him. His Gospel in the Church year Without Luke there would be no Christmas story as we tell it: the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Magnificat, the Benedictus, the shepherds, the Gloria in excelsis ( Luke 2:14 ), Simeon's Nunc dimittis . d: Franciscan preacher, finder of lost things
x: Home › Saints St Anthony of Padua Franciscan preacher, finder of lost things Saint Anthony of Padua with the Child , Bartolomé Esteban Murillo · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 1195–1231, Lisbon–Padua Feast day 13 June Recognised Canonised 1232 (Gregory IX); Doctor of the Church 1946 His story Born Fernando in Lisbon , he became an Augustinian canon, but the sight of the relics of the first Franciscan martyrs, killed in Morocco, made him join the Franciscans, taking the name Anthony. He sailed for Morocco, fell ill, and a storm drove his ship to Sicily. Called on unexpectedly to preach at an ordination, he astonished everyone; from then on he was a celebrated preacher in Italy and southern France, admired by Francis of Assisi himself. He died near Padua at about 36. Path to sainthood Canonised by Pope Gregory IX on 30 May 1232 , less than a year after his death, one of the fastest canonisations in history. Pope Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946. Patronages Lost things, the poor, Portugal, Padua. Trivia He is invoked for lost items because, according to a story, a novice who borrowed his psalter without permission returned it after Anthony prayed. A legend tells of him preaching to the fish at Rimini when the people would not listen. When his tomb was opened in 1263, his tongue was reportedly found incorrupt; it is displayed in the Basilica of St Anthony in Padua. Sources Benedict XVI, General Audience on St Anthony of Padua (10 Feb 2010), vati

d: Mystic, peacemaker and Doctor of the Church
x: Home › Saints St Catherine of Siena Mystic, peacemaker and Doctor of the Church St Catherine of Siena (c. 1746) , Giovanni Battista Tiepolo · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1347–1380, Siena–Rome Feast day 29 April Recognised Canonised 1461 (Pius II); Doctor of the Church 1970 Her story The 24th of 25 children of a Sienese dyer, Catherine refused marriage and became a Dominican tertiary, living a life of prayer and fasting at home before turning to care for the sick and poor. Though she learned to write only late, she dictated hundreds of letters to popes, kings and ordinary people, and a book of mystical theology, The Dialogue . She urged Pope Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome, which he did in 1377, and she worked for peace in the Church during the Western Schism. She died in Rome aged 33. The full story: dyer's daughter, mystic and Doctor of the Church History or legend? Catherine is one of the best-documented women of the Middle Ages. We have about 380 of her letters , her book, the Dialogue , and her prayers, along with the detailed Legenda Maior written by her confessor, Raymond of Capua , and testimony collected after her death. Her public role (Avignon, Florence, the Schism) is solid history. Her mystical experiences (the espousal, the exchange of hearts, the stigmata) are known almost entirely from Raymond's hagiography and her own reports. d: Soldier turned founder of the Jesuits
x: Home › Saints St Ignatius of Loyola Soldier turned founder of the Jesuits Saint Ignatius of Loyola (c. 1620) , Peter Paul Rubens · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1491–1556, Loyola–Rome Feast day 31 July Recognised Canonised 12 March 1622 (Gregory XV) His story Íñigo López de Loyola was a Basque nobleman and soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball during the defence of Pamplona in 1521. Recovering at Loyola with only lives of Christ and the saints to read, he was converted. He spent months praying in a cave at Manresa, where he drafted the Spiritual Exercises , then studied in Spain and Paris, where he gathered companions including Francis Xavier. In 1540 Pope Paul III approved their Society of Jesus. Ignatius ran it from Rome until his death, as the Jesuits spread schools and missions across the world. Path to sainthood Beatified in 1609 and canonised by Pope Gregory XV on 12 March 1622 , in the same ceremony as Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer. Patronages Soldiers, retreats, the Basque Country. Trivia The Jesuit motto Ad maiorem Dei gloriam ("for the greater glory of God") is often abbreviated AMDG . He laid down his sword before the Black Madonna at Montserrat in 1522, a scene inspired by the chivalric romances he loved. Pope Francis was the first Jesuit pope. d: Jesuit missionary to India and Japan
x: Home › Saints St Francis Xavier Jesuit missionary to India and Japan The Miracles of St Francis Xavier (1617–18) , Peter Paul Rubens · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1506–1552, Navarre–Shangchuan Feast day 3 December Recognised Canonised 12 March 1622 (Gregory XV) His story A Navarrese nobleman studying in Paris, Francis Xavier was won over by his roommate's friend Ignatius of Loyola and became one of the first Jesuits. In 1541 he sailed from Lisbon for Goa , then worked in southern India, Malacca and the Moluccas, and in 1549 reached Japan , where he founded the first Christian communities. He died of fever in 1552 on the island of Shangchuan , off the coast of China, waiting for a ship to take him to the mainland. Patronages Missions, missionaries, India, Japan, Navarre. Trivia His body lies in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa; his right arm, which baptised thousands, is kept in the Gesù church in Rome. His letters to Europe, describing Asia, were widely printed and inspired many missionaries. A legend says a crab returned his lost crucifix from the sea on the way to the Moluccas. d: Capuchin friar of the stigmata
x: Home › Saints St Pio of Pietrelcina (Padre Pio) Capuchin friar of the stigmata Padre Pio (photograph, c. 1947) , unknown photographer · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1887–1968, Pietrelcina–San Giovanni Rotondo Feast day 23 September Recognised Canonised 16 June 2002 (John Paul II) His story Francesco Forgione, from a farming family in Pietrelcina near Benevento, joined the Capuchins and was ordained in 1910. From 1916 he lived at the friary of San Giovanni Rotondo. On 20 September 1918 he reported receiving the stigmata , wounds like Christ's, which he bore for 50 years. Vast crowds came for his Masses and his confessions, and he was investigated and at times restricted by Church authorities. He founded the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza ("Home for the Relief of Suffering"), a hospital opened in 1956. Path to sainthood Beatified on 2 May 1999 and canonised by Pope John Paul II on 16 June 2002 . Patronages Civil defence volunteers, adolescents (popularly). Trivia As a young priest, Karol Wojtyła (the future John Paul II) went to confession to him in 1947. Many people reported extraordinary gifts such as bilocation and reading hearts; these are testimonies, not matters of faith. His body has been on display at San Giovanni Rotondo since 2008, one of Italy's most visited shrines. d: Franciscan who gave his life at Auschwitz
x: Home › Saints St Maximilian Kolbe Franciscan who gave his life at Auschwitz Fr Maximilian Kolbe (photograph, 1936) , unknown photographer · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1894–1941, Zduńska Wola–Auschwitz Feast day 14 August Recognised Canonised 10 October 1982 (John Paul II), as a martyr His story Raymund Kolbe became a Conventual Franciscan, taking the name Maximilian. He founded the Militia of the Immaculata, a huge Catholic press, and the friary-town of Niepokalanów near Warsaw, and spent years as a missionary in Nagasaki, Japan. Arrested by the Gestapo, he was sent to Auschwitz in 1941. When ten prisoners were chosen to starve to death in reprisal for an escape, he volunteered to take the place of Franciszek Gajowniczek , who cried out that he had a wife and children. After two weeks in the starvation bunker, Kolbe was killed with a lethal injection on 14 August 1941 . Path to sainthood Beatified in 1971 by Pope Paul VI and canonised by Pope John Paul II on 10 October 1982 , as a martyr of charity. Patronages Drug addicts, prisoners, journalists, families, the pro-life movement. Trivia Franciszek Gajowniczek survived the war and attended both the beatification and the canonisation; he died in 1995. Kolbe had a lively interest in science and sketched ideas for a spacecraft as a young man. His starvation cell (Block 11) at Auschwitz is a place of pilgrimage. Sources John Paul II, Homily at the canonization of Maximilian Kolbe (10 Oct 1982), vatican.va (Italian)

d: Lawyer, scholar and martyr for conscience
x: Home › Saints St Thomas More Lawyer, scholar and martyr for conscience Sir Thomas More (1527) , Hans Holbein the Younger · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1478–1535, London Feast day 22 June (with St John Fisher) Recognised Canonised 19 May 1935 (Pius XI) His story A brilliant London lawyer and humanist, friend of Erasmus and author of Utopia (1516), Thomas More rose to become Lord Chancellor of England under Henry VIII in 1529. He resigned in 1532 as the king broke with Rome over his marriage, and refused to swear the oath recognising Henry's supremacy over the Church in England. Imprisoned in the Tower of London, he was convicted of treason and beheaded on 6 July 1535 . Tradition records his last words as declaring he died "the King's good servant, but God's first". Path to sainthood Beatified in 1886 and canonised by Pope Pius XI on 19 May 1935 , together with Bishop John Fisher. Pope John Paul II proclaimed him patron of statesmen and politicians in 2000. Patronages Statesmen, politicians, lawyers, adopted children. Trivia His life inspired Robert Bolt's play and film A Man for All Seasons . He wore a hair shirt under his chancellor's robes; one survives. His head was displayed on London Bridge; his daughter Margaret Roper is said to have rescued it, and tradition says it lies in a family vault in Canterbury. Sources John Paul II, motu proprio proclaiming St Thomas More patron of statesmen (31 Oct 2000), vatican.va Catholic Encyclopedia: St Thomas More Fact-che

d: Translator of the Bible into Latin
x: Home › Saints St Jerome Translator of the Bible into Latin Saint Jerome Writing (1605–06) , Caravaggio · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 347–420, Stridon–Bethlehem Feast day 30 September Recognised Pre-Congregation; Doctor of the Church His story Born in Stridon on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia, Jerome studied in Rome, tried the hermit life in the Syrian desert, learned Hebrew, and became secretary to Pope Damasus, who asked him to revise the Latin Gospels. After Damasus's death he settled in Bethlehem , where with the help of Roman noblewomen Paula and Eustochium he founded monasteries and spent decades translating the Old Testament from Hebrew. His work became the core of the Vulgate , the Latin Bible used in the West for over a thousand years. He was also famous for a fierce temper and sharp pen. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint; one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church (with Ambrose, Augustine and Gregory the Great). Patronages Translators, librarians, scholars. Trivia His saying " Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ " is quoted by the Second Vatican Council. The legend of Jerome pulling a thorn from a lion's paw was probably borrowed from the story of St Gerasimus; that's why painters show him with a lion. International Translation Day is celebrated on 30 September , his feast day. d: The mother who prayed for Augustine
x: Home › Saints St Monica The mother who prayed for Augustine Saints Augustine and Monica (1854) , Ary Scheffer · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 331–387, Thagaste–Ostia Feast day 27 August Recognised Pre-Congregation Her story We know Monica almost entirely through the Confessions of her son, St Augustine of Hippo . A Christian from Thagaste in North Africa, married to a pagan with a hot temper, she prayed and wept for years for her brilliant, wayward son. A bishop reassured her that "the son of these tears" would not be lost. She followed Augustine to Italy and saw him baptised in Milan in 387. On the way home, at the port of Ostia, mother and son shared a famous moment of contemplation at a window; she died there days later. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint, venerated especially from the Middle Ages. Patronages Mothers, wives, patience, alcoholics (tradition). Trivia The city of Santa Monica , California, is named after her. Her tombstone inscription was found at Ostia in 1945. Her feast falls the day before her son's (28 August). d: Founder of the Poor Clares, Francis's companion
x: Home › Saints St Clare of Assisi Founder of the Poor Clares, Francis's companion Saint Clare (c. 1320) , Simone Martini · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1194–1253, Assisi Feast day 11 August Recognised Canonised 1255 (Alexander IV) Her story A young noblewoman of Assisi, Clare was moved by Francis's preaching. On the night of Palm Sunday 1212 she slipped away from home, and at the Portiuncula Francis cut her hair and gave her a rough habit. She settled at San Damiano , where she led a community of women in strict poverty for over 40 years, often ill but never giving up what she called the "privilege of poverty". Her sisters, the Poor Clares , spread across Europe. Path to sainthood Canonised by Pope Alexander IV in 1255 , only two years after her death. Patronages Television, eye disease, embroiderers. Trivia Two days before she died, Pope Innocent IV approved her Rule, the first rule known to have been written by a woman. Pope Pius XII named her patron of television in 1958, because when she was too ill to attend Mass she reportedly saw and heard it on the wall of her room. Tradition says she turned back Saracen soldiers attacking San Damiano by holding up the Blessed Sacrament. d: Roman martyr, the saint shot with arrows
x: Home › Saints St Sebastian Roman martyr, the saint shot with arrows Saint Sebastian (c. 1457–59) , Andrea Mantegna · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 288, Rome Feast day 20 January Recognised Pre-Congregation His story Sebastian was a Christian martyr of Rome, buried on the Appian Way where the Basilica of San Sebastiano now stands; St Ambrose mentions him in the 4th century. The famous story comes from a later Passio (5th century) and is legend: an officer in the imperial guard, he was shot with arrows on the emperor's orders, nursed back to health by a widow named Irene, and then confronted the emperor and was clubbed to death. The arrows and the recovery: the full story History or legend? Only three things are early and solid. The Depositio Martyrum (a list of Roman martyrs' burial feasts in the Chronograph of 354) records: "XIII Kal. Feb. … Sebastiani in Catacumbas", meaning Sebastian was honoured on 20 January at the cemetery "ad Catacumbas" on the Appian Way. St Ambrose (d. 397), commenting on Psalm 118, says Sebastian was a native of Milan who was martyred in Rome. And a basilica stood over his tomb by the 4th century. Everything else below, the soldier, the arrows, Irene and the club, comes from the Passio Sancti Sebastiani , a long, dramatic text written in the early 5th century , about 120 years later, and once wrongly credited to Ambrose. d: Roman martyr behind Valentine's Day
x: Home › Saints St Valentine Roman martyr behind Valentine's Day St Valentine Baptizing St Lucilla (c. 1575) , Jacopo Bassano · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. 3rd century (c. 269?), Rome Feast day 14 February (local; Roman Martyrology) Recognised Pre-Congregation; removed from the General Calendar in 1969 His story Early sources record a martyr named Valentine buried on the Via Flaminia north of Rome; another tradition speaks of a bishop Valentine of Terni, and the two may be the same person. Beyond that, very little is known. Later legends say he healed a jailer's daughter and signed a farewell note "from your Valentine", or secretly married couples against the emperor's orders; these stories have no early source. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint. Because so little is known, his feast was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969 , but he remains in the Roman Martyrology and is still honoured locally. Patronages Lovers, engaged couples, beekeepers, epilepsy. Trivia The link between his day and romantic love first appears in late-medieval English poetry, notably Chaucer's Parlement of Foules (14th century). Relics said to be his are claimed by several churches, including in Rome, Terni and Dublin's Whitefriar Street church. On 14 February the General Calendar today celebrates Sts Cyril and Methodius , apostles to the Slavs. Sources Vatican News: St Valentine Catholic Encyclopedia: St Valentine Fact-checked on October 15, 2026 against Vatican documen

d: Witness of Our Lady of Guadalupe
x: Home › Saints St Juan Diego Witness of Our Lady of Guadalupe The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Juan Diego's tilma (1531) , Basilica of Guadalupe · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1474–1548, Mexico Feast day 9 December Recognised Canonised 31 July 2002 (John Paul II) His story Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin was an Indigenous (Nahua) convert in central Mexico. According to the tradition first written down in the 16th century in the Nahuatl Nican Mopohua , in December 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared to him on the hill of Tepeyac , asking that a church be built there. When the bishop asked for a sign, Juan Diego gathered roses out of season in his cloak ( tilma ); when he opened it before the bishop, the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe was found on it. Some historians questioned whether he existed; the Church concluded its investigation in favour of his historicity. Patronages Indigenous peoples (popularly). Trivia His tilma with the image hangs in the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City, one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world. Our Lady of Guadalupe's feast is 12 December, three days after his. The image shows Mary with dark skin and Indigenous features, a powerful symbol for Mexico. d: "Lily of the Mohawks", first Native American saint
x: Home › Saints St Kateri Tekakwitha "Lily of the Mohawks", first Native American saint Kateri Tekakwitha (c. 1690) , Fr Claude Chauchetière · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1656–1680, Ossernenon–Kahnawake Feast day 14 July (USA); 17 April (Canada) Recognised Canonised 21 October 2012 (Benedict XVI) Her story Tekakwitha was born at Ossernenon, a Mohawk village in what is now New York State, to a Mohawk father and an Algonquin Christian mother. Smallpox killed her parents and left her face scarred and her eyesight weak. Drawn to the faith by Jesuit missionaries, she was baptised at 20 and took the name Kateri (Catherine). Facing hostility at home, she fled to the Christian mission of Kahnawake near Montreal, where she lived a life of prayer, penance and care for others before dying at 24. Path to sainthood Beatified on 22 June 1980 by Pope John Paul II and canonised by Pope Benedict XVI on 21 October 2012 , the first Indigenous North American saint. Patronages Ecology and the environment, Indigenous peoples. Trivia Witnesses said her smallpox scars disappeared shortly after her death; this is reported by the Jesuits who knew her. The earliest portrait of her, by Fr Claude Chauchetière, was painted from memory around 1690. Her shrine is at the St Francis Xavier church in Kahnawake, Quebec. d: Teenage computer whiz, the first millennial saint
x: Home › Saints St Carlo Acutis Teenage computer whiz, the first millennial saint Carlo Acutis memorial, Corpus Christi Church, Covent Garden (photo) , AndyScott · CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1991–2006, London–Monza Feast day 12 October Recognised Canonised 7 September 2025 (Leo XIV) His story Born in London to Italian parents and raised in Milan, Carlo Acutis loved video games, football and computers, and taught himself programming. He went to Mass daily from his First Communion, and built a website and exhibition cataloguing Eucharistic miracles around the world, which has since travelled to many countries. He died of acute leukaemia on 12 October 2006 , aged 15, offering his suffering for the Pope and the Church. He is buried in Assisi , at the Sanctuary of the Spoliation. Path to sainthood Beatified in Assisi on 10 October 2020. His canonisation, first set for 27 April 2025, was postponed after Pope Francis died on 21 April 2025. Pope Leo XIV canonised him on 7 September 2025 , together with Pier Giorgio Frassati. Patronages The internet (popularly proposed), young people. Trivia He called the Eucharist " my highway to Heaven ". He was born on 3 May 1991, making him the first saint of the millennial generation. At his tomb in Assisi he is displayed in jeans, sweatshirt and trainers. d: The peacemaker queen of the roses
x: Home › Saints St Elizabeth of Portugal The peacemaker queen of the roses Saint Elizabeth of Portugal (c. 1635) , Francisco de Zurbarán · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1271–1336, Zaragoza–Estremoz Feast day 4 July Recognised Canonised 25 May 1625 (Urban VIII) Place Coimbra, Portugal Her story Isabel was born a princess of Aragon, probably in Zaragoza, and named after her great-aunt St Elizabeth of Hungary. At 12 she was married to King Dinis of Portugal , a gifted ruler but an unfaithful husband. She raised his children by other women as well as her own, kept a strict life of prayer, and gave generously to the poor, to hospitals and to convents. She became famous as a peacemaker . When civil war broke out between Dinis and their son Afonso, she rode out between the two armies at Alvalade in 1323 and brought them to terms. She did the same between Portugal and Castile, and between her son and his own sons, and was making a peace journey when she died at Estremoz in 1336. After Dinis's death in 1325 she walked as a pilgrim to Santiago de Compostela and gave her crown to the cathedral. She then lived beside the Poor Clare convent she had founded in Coimbra, as a Franciscan tertiary. ( Coimbra lies on the Camino Portugués .) The miracle of the roses (legend): Dinis, the story goes, caught her carrying bread to the poor in her skirt, against his wishes, and demanded to see. d: Portugal's Holy Constable, soldier turned Carmelite
x: Home › Saints St Nuno Álvares Pereira Portugal's Holy Constable, soldier turned Carmelite King John I visits Nuno Álvares Pereira at the Carmo Convent in 1425 (1883) , Caetano Moreira da Costa Lima · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1360–1431, Cernache do Bonjardim–Lisbon Feast day 6 November Recognised Canonised 26 April 2009 (Benedict XVI) Place Lisbon, Portugal His story Nuno Álvares Pereira was a nobleman who, still in his twenties, became the Constable (commander-in-chief) of Portugal during the crisis of 1383–85, when Castile tried to take the Portuguese throne. Backing John of Aviz, he won a string of victories, above all the Battle of Aljubarrota on 14 August 1385, where a small Portuguese army with English archers defeated a much larger Castilian force and secured Portugal's independence. The victory was commemorated by the great monastery at Batalha. He was known as a soldier who prayed before battle, forbade looting and treated the defeated with mercy. In 1389 he founded the Carmelite convent of Carmo in Lisbon. After his wife and only daughter died, he gave away his vast estates and in 1423 entered the convent as a humble lay brother, Brother Nuno of Saint Mary , begging in the streets for the poor. He died there on 1 April 1431, Easter Sunday. The history here is well documented by contemporary chroniclers such as Fernão Lopes. Later popular tradition added miracles at Aljubarrota, such as a spring that appeared for his thirsty troops. Path to sainthood

d: Founder of the Hospitallers, patron of the sick
x: Home › Saints St John of God Founder of the Hospitallers, patron of the sick Saint John of God Carrying a Sick Man (c. 1672) , Bartolomé Esteban Murillo · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1495–1550, Montemor-o-Novo–Granada Feast day 8 March Recognised Canonised 16 October 1690 (Alexander VIII) Place Montemor-o-Novo / Granada, Portugal & Spain His story João Cidade was born in Montemor-o-Novo in Portugal and, as a boy, ended up in Spain, where he worked as a shepherd, served as a soldier, and later sold books and holy pictures in Granada . In 1537 a sermon by the preacher St John of Ávila shook him so deeply that he ran through the streets, gave away his books and behaved so wildly that he was locked up in the Royal Hospital as a madman. There he saw how the mentally ill were treated, chained and whipped. Once released, he rented a house and began caring for the sick and homeless himself, begging at night with the cry, " Do good, brothers, to yourselves! " His followers became the Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God , now running hospitals in more than 50 countries. He died in Granada on his 55th birthday, after diving into a river to save a drowning boy. Most of his life is well attested by an early biography (1585). Some details, such as the Child Jesus giving him the name "John of God" and the city of Granada as his destiny, come from pious tradition. d: The child seers of Fátima
x: Home › Saints Sts Francisco and Jacinta Marto The child seers of Fátima Francisco and Jacinta Marto (photograph, 1917) , unknown photographer · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived Francisco 1908–1919; Jacinta 1910–1920 Feast day 20 February Recognised Canonised 13 May 2017 (Francis) Place Fátima, Portugal Their story Francisco and Jacinta Marto were a brother and sister from the hamlet of Aljustrel, near Fátima in central Portugal. With their cousin Lúcia dos Santos they looked after their families' sheep. Between 13 May and 13 October 1917 , the three children reported six apparitions of a Lady "brighter than the sun" at the Cova da Iria, asking for prayer, especially the rosary, and penance for sinners. Crowds grew month by month despite official hostility; the children were even jailed and threatened for a time. On 13 October, tens of thousands of people reported seeing the sun spin and plunge, the " Miracle of the Sun ", reported in the Portuguese secular press. Both children caught the Spanish flu in the 1918 pandemic. Francisco, quiet and contemplative, died at home on 4 April 1919, aged ten; Jacinta, who offered many sacrifices for sinners, died alone in a Lisbon hospital on 20 February 1920, aged nine. The apparitions are approved by the Church as "worthy of belief" (1930), which means Catholics may believe them, not that they must. The solar phenomenon is documented by many witnesses, but there is no scientific explanation and it was not seen by observatories.

d: Deacon martyr, patron of Lisbon and Valencia
x: Home › Saints St Vincent of Saragossa Deacon martyr, patron of Lisbon and Valencia The Apotheosis of Saint Vincent of Saragossa , Carlo Innocenzo Carlone · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. 304, Valencia Feast day 22 January Recognised Pre-Congregation Place Lisbon / Valencia, Portugal & Spain His story Vincent was a deacon of the church of Saragossa (Zaragoza) under Bishop Valerius, who had a speech impediment and let Vincent preach for him. In the persecution of Diocletian, both were arrested and taken to Valencia . Valerius was exiled; Vincent was tortured on the rack and a gridiron and died in prison in 304. The poet Prudentius wrote a hymn to him around 400, and St Augustine preached several sermons on his feast, so his martyrdom is early and well attested. His later fame owes much to legend. His body, thrown to the wild animals, was said to be guarded by a raven ; thrown into the sea, it washed ashore. Christians later took it to the southwestern tip of Portugal, which is still called Cape St Vincent . The ravens of Lisbon (legend): In 1173 King Afonso Henriques had the relics brought by ship from the cape to Lisbon, and two ravens are said to have kept watch on the ship the whole way. A ship with two ravens has been Lisbon's coat of arms ever since, and you can see it on the city's lamp-posts and bins. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint, one of the most celebrated martyrs of the early Church in the West. Patronages Lisbon, Valencia, wine-growers (vint

AD 44, Jerusalem Feast day 25 July Recognised Pre-Congregation (apostle) Place Santiago de Compostela, Spain His story James, son of Zebedee and brother of John the Apostle , was a Galilean fisherman called by Jesus from his nets (Mark 1:19–20). With Peter and John he was one of the inner three, present at the Transfiguration and in Gethsemane. Jesus called the brothers "sons of thunder". He is called "the Greater" to tell him apart from the other apostle James. He is the only apostle whose death is recorded in the New Testament: King Herod Agrippa I "had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword" (Acts 12:2), around AD 44. That is history. Santiago (tradition and legend): A tradition first written down in the 7th century says James preached in Spain, and that after his martyrdom his disciples brought his body by boat to Galicia. In the early 9th century a hermit named Pelagius saw lights over a field, and Bishop Theodemir of Iria Flavia identified a Roman-era tomb there as the apostle's. King Alfonso II built a church, and Santiago de Compostela became, with Rome and Jerusalem, one of the three great pilgrimages of Christendom. d: Labourer and patron saint of Madrid
x: Home › Saints St Isidore the Farmer Labourer and patron saint of Madrid Saint Isidore the Farmer , Cuzco School · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 1070–1130, Madrid Feast day 15 May Recognised Canonised 12 March 1622 (Gregory XV) Place Madrid, Spain His story Isidore was a poor farm labourer who worked the fields of a landowner, Juan de Vargas, near Madrid , then a small town. He married María Toribia , also venerated as a saint (Santa María de la Cabeza). He went to Mass every morning before work, shared his meagre food with the poor and even with birds, and lived a simple, holy life. He died around 1130 and was buried in the cemetery of San Andrés. Madrid's devotion grew after his body was moved into the church in the 12th century and was found incorrupt. The angels who ploughed (legend): His fellow workers complained that he came late because of Mass. His master went to check and saw two angels ploughing beside Isidore, so that he did three men's work. Another story has him make a spring gush from the dry ground with his staff, and another says his son fell into a well and was saved when the water rose up to the brim. These come from a 13th-century life written long after his death. Path to sainthood Canonised by Pope Gregory XV on 12 March 1622 , in the same ceremony as Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila and Philip Neri. King Philip III, who believed he had been cured through Isidore's relics in 1619, pushed for the canonisation. Patronages M

d: Poet of the Dark Night, Teresa's companion
x: Home › Saints St John of the Cross Poet of the Dark Night, Teresa's companion Christ Appears to St John of the Cross (19th century) , Robert von Langer, Bavarian State Painting Collections · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1542–1591, Fontiveros–Úbeda Feast day 14 December Recognised Canonised 27 December 1726 (Benedict XIII); Doctor of the Church 1926 Place Segovia / Úbeda, Spain His story Juan de Yepes grew up in poverty in Castile; his father died when he was small. He became a Carmelite friar and was ordained in 1567, the year he met St Teresa of Ávila , who persuaded the young friar to join her reform. In 1568 he helped found the first friary of the Discalced (barefoot) Carmelites at Duruelo, taking the name John of the Cross. The reform caused bitter conflict. In December 1577 friars opposed to it kidnapped John and locked him in a tiny cell in their priory at Toledo for nine months, flogging him regularly. In that darkness he composed much of his poem the Spiritual Canticle . In August 1578 he escaped by night down a rope of knotted strips of blanket. He went on to lead and found friaries in Andalusia, and wrote the Dark Night of the Soul , the Ascent of Mount Carmel and the Living Flame of Love , which are masterpieces of Spanish poetry and mystical theology. Sidelined again at the end of his life, he died at Úbeda on 14 December 1591. His life is well documented. Pious tradition adds details such as Mary helping him escape from Toledo. d: Legendary first bishop of Pamplona, saint of the bull-run
x: Home › Saints St Fermín Legendary first bishop of Pamplona, saint of the bull-run The Martyrdom of Saint Fermín (1751) , Mauricio García · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 303 (tradition), Amiens Feast day 7 July (Pamplona; until 1591, 10 October) Recognised Pre-Congregation; historicity uncertain Place Pamplona, Spain His story Very little about Fermín (Latin Firminus ) is historically certain. A bishop named Firminus was venerated as a martyr at Amiens in northern France from early times. The link with Pamplona comes from a later tradition, written down in the Middle Ages. The Pamplona tradition (legend): Fermín was the son of a Roman senator of Pamplona named Firmus. He was converted by the priest Honestus, a disciple sent by St Saturninus (Sernin) of Toulouse, and baptised; a well in Pamplona is still pointed out as the place. He became the city's first bishop, preached in Gaul and was beheaded at Amiens. His cult in Pamplona really began in 1186 , when Bishop Pedro de París brought a fragment of his skull from Amiens; it is kept in a silver bust in Pamplona Cathedral. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint, known from liturgical tradition rather than reliable records. He is co-patron of Navarre with St Francis Xavier (made official in the 1650s). Pamplona's official patron is in fact St Saturninus; Fermín is its patron by popular devotion. Patronages Pamplona, Navarre (co-patron), bakers, wine-makers. d: Girl martyr of Mérida and Barcelona
x: Home › Saints St Eulalia Girl martyr of Mérida and Barcelona Saint Eulalia (1885) , John William Waterhouse · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 304, Mérida Feast day 10 December (Mérida); 12 February (Barcelona) Recognised Pre-Congregation Place Mérida / Barcelona, Spain Her story Eulalia of Mérida was a girl of about 12 who, during the persecution of Diocletian, slipped away from her family's country house and presented herself to the Roman governor, denouncing the worship of idols. She was tortured and burned to death. The poet Prudentius , writing around 400, devoted a hymn ( Peristephanon III) to her: he says a white dove flew from her mouth as she died and that snow fell to cover her body. Her tomb in Mérida was a great pilgrimage site in late antiquity, and her basilica stands on it. Barcelona honours its own St Eulalia, a 13-year-old said to have suffered 13 tortures under Diocletian, including being rolled down a street in a barrel of glass and nails and crucified on an X-shaped cross. The Mérida martyr is early and well attested (Prudentius, early calendars). Most historians think Eulalia of Barcelona is a local copy of the Mérida saint whose story grew in the 7th century, though Barcelona venerates her separately. Her relics were placed in the crypt of Barcelona Cathedral in 1339. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint, among the most venerated martyrs of Roman Spain. Patronages Mérida, Barcelona (co-patron), sailors, against drought. Where to visit

d: Encyclopedist, bishop and Doctor of the Church
x: Home › Saints St Isidore of Seville Encyclopedist, bishop and Doctor of the Church Saint Isidore of Seville (1655) , Bartolomé Esteban Murillo · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 560–636, Cartagena?–Seville Feast day 4 April Recognised Pre-Congregation; Doctor of the Church 1722 Place Seville / León, Spain His story Isidore came from a family of saints: his brothers Leander and Fulgentius were bishops, and his sister Florentina an abbess. Raised by Leander after their parents died, he succeeded him as bishop of Seville around 600 and led the Church in Visigothic Spain for over three decades. He presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), which set out church discipline and urged a school attached to every cathedral. He is remembered above all for the Etymologies , a 20-book encyclopedia that tried to gather all knowledge, from grammar and medicine to geography and theology, organised around the origins of words. It was one of the most-copied books of the Middle Ages and passed classical learning on to medieval Europe. He also wrote histories of the Goths, Vandals and Suevi, and works of theology. His life is well documented. A pleasant legend says that as a baby a swarm of bees settled on his mouth, foretelling his eloquence (the same story is told of St Ambrose). Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint, venerated soon after his death. Pope Innocent XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1722. Patronages Students, (unofficially) the internet and comput

d: Founder of Opus Dei
x: Home › Saints St Josemaría Escrivá Founder of Opus Dei Torreciudad Sanctuary (photo) , Preyes · CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1902–1975, Barbastro–Rome Feast day 26 June Recognised Canonised 6 October 2002 (John Paul II) Place Barbastro / Torreciudad, Spain His story Josemaría Escrivá was born in Barbastro , Aragon. His family's business failed when he was a boy, and they moved to Logroño, where, he said, seeing footprints of a barefoot friar in the snow moved him to the priesthood. He was ordained in Zaragoza in 1925 and moved to Madrid. On 2 October 1928 , during a retreat, he said he "saw" what God wanted of him: Opus Dei ("Work of God"), an institution teaching that ordinary people can become saints through their daily work and family life. During the Spanish Civil War, when priests were being killed, he hid in Madrid and escaped across the Pyrenees in 1937. He published The Way ( Camino ), a book of short spiritual points, in 1939; it has sold millions of copies. He moved to Rome in 1946 and died there on 26 June 1975. By then Opus Dei had tens of thousands of members worldwide. His life is recent and documented. His canonisation was controversial : critics of Opus Dei objected to the speed of the process and questioned his personality and the organisation's secrecy, while supporters point to the many testimonies of holiness. d: "Slave of the slaves forever"
x: Home › Saints St Peter Claver "Slave of the slaves forever" Church of San Pedro Claver, Cartagena (photo) , Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1580–1654, Verdú–Cartagena Feast day 9 September Recognised Canonised 15 January 1888 (Leo XIII) Place Verdú / Cartagena de Indias, Spain & Colombia His story Pere Claver was born in Verdú in Catalonia and joined the Jesuits. On Majorca he met the elderly doorkeeper St Alphonsus Rodríguez , who urged him to go to the Americas. In 1610 he arrived at Cartagena de Indias (now Colombia), the main port for the transatlantic slave trade in Spanish America, and was ordained there in 1616. For nearly 40 years he met every slave ship as it docked, going down into the holds with food, water, medicine and interpreters, caring for the sick and dying, baptising, teaching and defending enslaved Africans. At his final vows he signed himself Petrus Claver, aethiopum semper servus ("Peter Claver, slave of the Africans forever"). He is said to have baptised about 300,000 people. He also visited prisoners and lepers. Paralysed by illness for his last four years and largely neglected, he died on 8 September 1654. His life is well documented from the testimony of his companions. Some miracle stories collected for his canonisation are pious tradition. Path to sainthood Beatified in 1850 and canonised by Pope Leo XIII on 15 January 1888 , together with Alphonsus Rodríguez. Leo XIII named him patron of missions to Africans in 1896. Pat

d: Bishop martyr of Naples and the blood miracle
x: Home › Saints St Januarius (San Gennaro) Bishop martyr of Naples and the blood miracle San Gennaro Emerges Unharmed from the Furnace (1646), Naples Cathedral , Jusepe de Ribera · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 305, Pozzuoli Feast day 19 September Recognised Pre-Congregation Place Naples, Italy His story Januarius (Gennaro) was bishop of Benevento and was martyred near Pozzuoli , by the Bay of Naples, around 305 under Diocletian, together with companions. Little more is known for certain; his cult is early, and his remains were brought to the catacombs of Naples in the 5th century, now named after him. The legend: His later Acts say he was thrown into a furnace and came out unharmed, then exposed to wild beasts in the amphitheatre of Pozzuoli, which would not touch him, before being beheaded at the Solfatara volcanic crater. The blood: Naples cathedral keeps two glass ampoules said to contain his dried blood. Three times a year (the Saturday before the first Sunday of May, 19 September, and 16 December), the archbishop holds them up, and the dark solid mass usually liquefies , sometimes within minutes, sometimes after hours of prayer. The first record is from 1389 . The Church allows the devotion but has never officially declared it a miracle ; it calls it a prodigio . Scientists have proposed natural explanations, such as a thixotropic gel, but the ampoules have never been opened for testing. Neapolitans see a failure to liquefy as a bad omen. Path to sainth

She wanted to be a nun, but her parents married her young to Paolo Mancini, a violent man. Over the years, her patience is said to have changed him, but he was murdered in a feud. Rita forgave the killers and, the tradition says, prayed that her two sons would die rather than avenge their father; both died of illness soon after. Alone, she asked to join the Augustinian convent of St Mary Magdalene at Cascia. She was refused at first, because of the feud, until she made peace between the families. She lived there for 40 years in prayer and penance. Much of her life comes from a biography written in 1628, 170 years after her death, and contains legend. The thorn: In 1442, praying before a crucifix, she received a wound on her forehead like a thorn from Christ's crown, which stayed open until her death. The rose and figs: On her deathbed in winter she asked for a rose and two figs from her old garden at Roccaporena, and a cousin found them blooming in the snow. d: Bishop of Milan, Doctor of the Church
x: Home › Saints St Ambrose Bishop of Milan, Doctor of the Church Saint Ambrose (c. 1465) , Giovanni di Paolo, Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 339–397, Trier–Milan Feast day 7 December Recognised Pre-Congregation; Doctor of the Church Place Milan, Italy His story Ambrose was born in Trier , the son of a high Roman official, trained as a lawyer and became governor of the province based at Milan . In 374, when the city's bishop died, Arian and Catholic factions fought over the succession. Ambrose came to the cathedral to keep order, and the crowd began to shout " Ambrose for bishop! " He was still only a catechumen. Within about a week he was baptised, ordained and consecrated. He became one of the great bishops of history: a brilliant preacher, a writer of hymns still sung today, and a defender of the Church against the Arians and imperial power. In 386 he and his people occupied a basilica the empress wanted for the Arians, singing hymns night and day. In 390 he made Emperor Theodosius do public penance for the massacre at Thessalonica. His preaching helped convert St Augustine , whom he baptised at the Easter Vigil of 387. His life was written by his secretary Paulinus soon after his death, so it is well documented. Legend: a swarm of bees settled on his face as a baby, a sign of his honeyed eloquence. Another tradition says that at his election a child's voice first cried "Ambrose bishop!" d: Gospel writer and patron of Venice
x: Home › Saints St Mark the Evangelist Gospel writer and patron of Venice Saint Mark Preaching in Alexandria (1504–07) , Gentile and Giovanni Bellini · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1st century; d. c. AD 68 (tradition), Alexandria Feast day 25 April Recognised Pre-Congregation (evangelist) Place Venice, Italy His story Mark is traditionally identified with John Mark of the Acts of the Apostles: his mother's house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the first Christians (Acts 12:12). He travelled with Paul and his cousin Barnabas, left them partway, and was later reconciled with Paul (Colossians 4:10). Peter calls him "my son Mark" (1 Peter 5:13). Around AD 120, Papias wrote that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down what Peter remembered of Jesus. His Gospel is the shortest and probably the earliest of the four. Tradition says he founded the Church of Alexandria in Egypt and was martyred there. The theft of the body (828): Two Venetian merchants, Buono of Malamocco and Rustico of Torcello, are said to have smuggled his body out of Alexandria by hiding it under pork , which the Muslim customs officials would not touch, and brought it to Venice. The story is told in the mosaics of St Mark's Basilica. Earlier, according to another legend, an angel had greeted Mark in the Venetian lagoon: Pax tibi, Marce, evangelista meus ("Peace to you, Mark, my evangelist"), the words on the book held by the Venetian lion. d: Hermit of Monte Pellegrino, saviour of Palermo
x: Home › Saints St Rosalia Hermit of Monte Pellegrino, saviour of Palermo Saint Rosalia Interceding for Palermo (1624) , Anthony van Dyck · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 1130–1166?, Palermo Feast day 4 September; 15 July (Festino) Recognised Pre-Congregation; in the Roman Martyrology since 1630 Place Palermo, Italy Her story According to Palermo tradition, Rosalia was a young noblewoman of the Sinibaldi family, related to the Norman royal house, who left the court to live as a hermit, first in a cave at Quisquina in the mountains and then in a cave on Monte Pellegrino , the headland above Palermo, where she died alone. For centuries she was little known. The plague of 1624 (history and legend): In 1624, as plague struck Palermo, a woman reported a vision of Rosalia, and on 15 July 1624 bones were found in the cave on Monte Pellegrino. A hunter named Vincenzo Bonello then said Rosalia had appeared to him, asking that her relics be carried through the city. When they were carried in procession in 1625, the plague receded, and Palermo made her its patroness. Her life story before 1624 rests mostly on tradition, but a Latin inscription in the Quisquina cave, said to be hers, records her stay there. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint. Pope Urban VIII added her to the Roman Martyrology in 1630. Patronages Palermo, against plague and epidemics. x: Home › Saints St Agatha Virgin martyr and patroness of Catania Saint Agatha (c. 1630–33) , Francisco de Zurbarán · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. 251, Catania (Sicily) Feast day 5 February Recognised Pre-Congregation Place Catania, Italy Her story Agatha was a young Christian woman of Catania , on Sicily's east coast, martyred during the persecution of Decius in 251 . Her cult is very early: she is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and Pope Symmachus built a church in her honour in Rome around 500. That much is history. Her Acts (legend): Her later Acts say the governor Quintianus wanted her, and when she refused he had her handed to a brothel, then tortured, and her breasts cut off . St Peter appeared to heal her in prison. She was then rolled over burning coals, and an earthquake shook the city before she died in prison. A year later, so the story goes, the people of Catania held up her veil against a lava flow from Mount Etna , and it stopped. Her relics were taken to Constantinople in 1040 and brought back in 1126 by two soldiers, Gisliberto and Goselmo, who are said to have hidden them in quivers. d: Mystic of Lucca
x: Home › Saints St Gemma Galgani Mystic of Lucca Gemma Galgani (photograph, c. 1901–03) , unknown photographer · public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1878–1903, Borgo Nuovo di Camigliano–Lucca Feast day 11 April Recognised Canonised 2 May 1940 (Pius XII) Place Lucca, Italy Her story Gemma Galgani was born near Lucca , in Tuscany, the daughter of a pharmacist. Her mother died when she was seven; her father died bankrupt when she was 19, leaving the children in poverty. Gemma fell seriously ill with spinal tuberculosis and was given up by the doctors; in 1899 she recovered suddenly, attributing her cure to St Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows, a young Passionist. That same year, on 8 June 1899 , she reported receiving the stigmata , which appeared on Thursday evenings and Fridays. She said she saw and spoke with her guardian angel and with Jesus, and suffered attacks from the devil. Taken in by the kind Giannini family, she longed to become a Passionist nun, but was refused because of her health. She died of tuberculosis on Holy Saturday, 11 April 1903, aged 25. Her experiences are recorded in her diary and letters and in the testimony of her spiritual director, the Passionist Fr Germano Ruoppolo, who wrote her life. Some contemporaries, including doctors, were sceptical, and the Church canonised her for her heroic virtue, without ruling on her mystical phenomena. Path to sainthood Beatified in 1933 and canonised by Pope Pius XII on 2 May 1940 . Patronages Pharmacists, student

d: Teenage Cristero martyr
x: Home › Saints St José Sánchez del Río Teenage Cristero martyr Image of St José Sánchez del Río, Basilica of Guadalupe, Mexico City (photo) , José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1913–1928, Sahuayo Feast day 10 February Recognised Canonised 16 October 2016 (Francis) Place Sahuayo, Mexico His story José Luis Sánchez del Río grew up in Sahuayo , Michoacán, during the Cristero War (1926–29), a rebellion against the Mexican government's harsh anti-Catholic laws, which closed churches, expelled foreign priests and banned public worship. At 13 he joined the Cristero forces, despite his mother's objections, serving as a flag-bearer and helper. In a battle in February 1928, he gave his horse to a general whose mount had been killed and was captured. Held in Sahuayo's own parish church, which had been turned into a jail, he was offered his freedom if he renounced his faith, and refused. On 10 February 1928 the soles of his feet were cut, and he was forced to walk to the cemetery. There he was stabbed and shot, still crying out " ¡Viva Cristo Rey! " ("Long live Christ the King!"). He was 14. His martyrdom is documented by witnesses and letters he wrote to his mother. Some vivid details, such as tracing a cross in his own blood on the ground, come from later tradition. Path to sainthood Beatified in Guadalajara on 20 November 2005 and canonised by Pope Francis on 16 October 2016 . Patronages Young people, Mexican Catholic youth (popularly). As parish priest of his home town he built schools, a seminary, farm cooperatives and dams, and preached among the Indigenous Huichol people. When the government closed churches in 1926, he kept his seminary going in secret. On the day he died, the story goes, the withered fig tree in his family's yard turned green. d: Bishop of Veracruz who ministered in disguise
x: Home › Saints St Rafael Guízar y Valencia Bishop of Veracruz who ministered in disguise Portrait of St Rafael Guízar y Valencia (photo of a painting) , Nheyob · CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1878–1938, Cotija–Mexico City Feast day 6 June Recognised Canonised 15 October 2006 (Benedict XVI) Place Xalapa, Mexico His story Rafael Guízar y Valencia was born into a wealthy family in Cotija , Michoacán, and ordained in 1901. He was a tireless missionary preacher. During the Mexican Revolution, when priests were hunted, he moved among the soldiers and the wounded in disguise (as a junk dealer, a doctor, a musician) to hear confessions and give the last rites. Sentenced to death, he escaped to the United States, Guatemala and Cuba. Named bishop of Veracruz in 1919, he arrived to find the region devastated by an earthquake and threw himself into relief work. When persecution closed the seminaries, he kept his own running in secret in Mexico City for 15 years, training hundreds of priests. Repeatedly exiled and threatened, he died in Mexico City on 6 June 1938, worn out and poor, having given away everything. His life is well documented. Stories of his narrow escapes, told by those who knew him, have grown in the retelling. Path to sainthood Beatified by John Paul II in 1995 and canonised by Pope Benedict XVI on 15 October 2006 . d: The woman who rose from her coffin
x: Home › Saints St Christina the Astonishing The woman who rose from her coffin Artistic illustration in a Renaissance fresco style, created for The Daily Word; not a historical likeness. Christina rising from her coffin at her own funeral. Lived c. 1150–1224, Brustem and Sint-Truiden (Belgium) Feast day 24 July (local) Recognised Venerated locally; never formally canonised The story Christina was an orphaned peasant girl from Brustem , near Sint-Truiden in today's Belgium. Almost everything we know comes from a Life written about 1232 by the Dominican Thomas of Cantimpré , who said he had spoken with people who knew her. Cardinal Jacques de Vitry also mentions her. The full story The funeral According to Thomas, Christina died of a seizure at about 22. During her funeral Mass, in the open coffin, she sat up and rose to the rafters of the church. The congregation fled. The priest coaxed her down. She said she had seen hell, purgatory and heaven, and had been offered the choice of staying in heaven or returning to suffer for the souls in purgatory. She chose to return. A strange life She could not bear the smell of human beings, Thomas says, and climbed trees, church towers and rocks to escape it. She threw herself into ovens and freezing rivers, prayed balanced on fence posts, and was chained up by her family, who thought her mad. Later in life she grew calmer and was sought out for advice, including by Count Louis of Looz. She died at the convent of St Catherine in Sint-Truide

d: Thirty-seven years on top of a pillar

His penances were so extreme that his monastery asked him to leave. He lived as a hermit near Telanissos (Deir Semaan), east of Antioch, but crowds came to touch him and ask his prayers. To escape them he went up . Around 423 he built a small pillar; over the years it was raised until it was about 15–18 m high, with a small platform and railing at the top. He lived on it for some 37 years , until his death in 459. The full story An eyewitness Unusually, we have reports from people who saw him: the historian Theodoret of Cyrrhus , who knew him, and a Syriac Life written by his disciples. They say he preached twice a day from the top, settled disputes, wrote letters to emperors and bishops (Theodosius II and Leo I asked his advice), and converted many Bedouin. Food was sent up by ladder. Qal'at Sim'an After his death a huge cross-shaped basilica was built around the pillar, one of the great churches of the 5th century. Its ruins, at Qal'at Sim'an in northern Syria, are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site; the stump of the pillar is still there, worn down by pilgrims taking pieces. In August 258 the Emperor Valerian ordered the execution of bishops, priests and deacons. Sixtus was beheaded on 6 August; Lawrence died four days later. His feast has been kept on 10 August since the 4th century, and he is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass. The full story The treasures of the Church St Ambrose tells the best-known story. The prefect of Rome demanded the Church's treasures. Lawrence asked for three days, gave everything away to the poor, then brought the city's sick, blind, lame and destitute before the prefect: "These are the treasures of the Church." The gridiron Ambrose and the poet Prudentius say he was roasted alive on a gridiron, and that halfway through he told his executioners, "I'm done on this side. Turn me over." His humour under torture made him patron of cooks and, half-jokingly, of comedians. History or legend? His martyrdom in 258 and his burial on the Via Tiburtina are certain. d: "Good King Wenceslas", Duke of Bohemia
x: Home › Saints St Wenceslaus "Good King Wenceslas", Duke of Bohemia Saint Wenceslas at the Vintage, Attended by Angels and Putti by Franz Anton Maulbertsch, CC0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 907–935, Bohemia Feast day 28 September Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Wenceslaus (Václav) was Duke of Bohemia in the early 10th century. He was brought up a Christian by his grandmother, St Ludmila , who was murdered in 921, probably on the orders of his pagan-leaning mother. As duke he favoured the Church, made peace with the German king Henry the Fowler, and was remembered for charity to the poor. On 28 September 935 (or 929) he was murdered on his way to Mass at Stará Boleslav by followers of his brother Boleslaus , who took the throne. The full story Patron of a nation He was venerated as a martyr almost at once. His relics were taken to St Vitus's Cathedral in Prague, where the jewelled St Wenceslas Chapel holds his tomb, and he became the patron saint of the Czech lands. The equestrian statue in Wenceslas Square in Prague is where Czechs gathered in 1918, 1968 and 1989. A legend says he sleeps with an army of knights under Mount Blaník and will ride out when Bohemia is in its darkest hour. The carol The English carol "Good King Wenceslas" was written by John Mason Neale in 1853, set to a 13th-century spring tune. Disciples gathered, and the monastery he founded became one of the great monastic cities of Ireland, with churches, a round tower and a school. The devil appeared as a crow, crying " Cras! Cras! ", Latin for "tomorrow, tomorrow". Expeditus stamped on it and said " Hodie! ", "Today!" A cephalophore ("head-carrier"), he is shown holding his own head; a statue on the portal of Notre-Dame de Paris shows him so. Saint-Denis The Basilica of Saint-Denis was built over his tomb. It became the burial place of the kings of France and, under Abbot Suger in the 1140s, the birthplace of Gothic architecture. "Montjoie Saint-Denis!" was the French royal battle cry. History and legend. The martyrdom of a Bishop Denis of Paris in the 3rd century is historical. The walk with his head is legend. Genesius converting mid-performance before the emperor.
