Patronages Actors, comedians, clowns, musicians, dancers, converts. Trivia The St Genesius chapel in many theatres and the "Actors' Church" (St Paul's, Covent Garden) keep his memory

d: From gang leader to desert father
x: Home › Saints St Moses the Black From gang leader to desert father Saints Poimen, Elijah, and Moses the Black by Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 330–405, Egypt Feast day 28 August Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Moses was an Ethiopian (or Nubian) slave in Egypt who was dismissed by his master for theft and became the leader of a gang of robbers in the Nile valley, feared for his size and violence. Hiding from the law, he took refuge with the monks of Scetis (Wadi Natrun) in the desert. Their peace and kindness changed him. He became a monk, then a priest, and one of the best-loved of the Desert Fathers . The full story The leaking basket The Sayings of the Desert Fathers preserve stories about him. Once a council was called to judge a monk who had sinned. Moses refused to come, then arrived carrying a leaking basket full of sand. "What is this?" they asked. "My sins run out behind me, and I do not see them, and today I come to judge the sins of another." The monks forgave their brother. The robbers One night four robbers broke into his cell. Moses overpowered them, tied them up, and carried them to the other monks, asking what to do, since he was not allowed to hurt anyone. When they learned who he was, the robbers became monks too. Moses died around 405, killed with seven other monks by raiders; he refused to defend himself, saying: "All who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). History. Moses is known fro

d: From Alexandria's streets to 47 years in the desert
x: Home › Saints St Mary of Egypt From Alexandria's streets to 47 years in the desert Mary of Egypt british library by french, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 344–421, Alexandria and the Jordan desert Feast day 1 April (West); 5th Sunday of Lent (East) Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Her Life , attributed to St Sophronius of Jerusalem (7th century), says Mary left home at 12 and lived for 17 years in Alexandria as a dissolute woman, seeking pleasure, not money. Out of curiosity she joined a pilgrim ship to Jerusalem for the feast of the Holy Cross. The full story The invisible barrier At the door of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre she tried to enter with the crowd, but an invisible force held her back three times. Seeing an icon of the Virgin in the courtyard, she wept and promised to change her life. She then entered freely and venerated the Cross. A voice told her: "Cross the Jordan, and you will find rest." The desert She crossed the Jordan with three loaves and lived alone in the desert for 47 years . Near the end the monk Zosimas met her: she knew Scripture without having read it and seemed to walk on the Jordan. He brought her Communion. A year later he found her dead, with a message in the sand asking him to bury her; a lion helped dig the grave. History or legend? The Life is a much-loved spiritual story read in Orthodox churches every Lent. Historians regard many details as legendary, but the Church has long held her up as an example of repentance.

d: Father of monks, tempted by demons in the desert
x: Home › Saints St Anthony the Abbot Father of monks, tempted by demons in the desert Colmar - Unterlinden Museum - The Isenheim Altarpiece 1512-16 by Matthias Grünew by Txllxt TxllxT, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 251–356, Egypt Feast day 17 January Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Anthony was born to a wealthy Christian family in Upper Egypt. At about 20 he heard in church the words "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21). He did exactly that and went into the desert. He lived for many years in an abandoned fort and later on a mountain near the Red Sea, where the Monastery of St Anthony still stands. He died aged about 105. The full story The temptations His Life by St Athanasius , written just after his death, was a bestseller of the ancient world and helped spread monasticism everywhere. It tells how demons attacked Anthony with visions of wealth and lust, beat him and appeared as wild beasts, while he answered with prayer. These temptations inspired painters from Bosch and Grünewald to Dalí. The pig and the fire In the Middle Ages the Hospitallers of St Anthony cared for victims of "St Anthony's fire" (ergotism, a poisoning from mouldy rye). Their pigs were allowed to roam the streets with bells, which is why Anthony is shown with a pig and a bell, and why animals are blessed on his feast. History. Anthony is historical, and Athanasius knew him. The demon stories are told as spiritual combat. St Augusti

d: The holy tramp of Rome
x: Home › Saints St Benedict Joseph Labre The holy tramp of Rome Saint Benedict Joseph Labre (1748–1783)label QS:Len,"Saint Benedict Joseph Labre by Antonio Cavallucci, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1748–1783, France and Rome Feast day 16 April Canonised 1881, Leo XIII The story Benedict Joseph was the eldest of 15 children of a shopkeeper in Amettes , northern France. He tried to join the Trappists, Carthusians and Cistercians, and was turned away by all of them as too young, too odd, or too sickly. The full story A pilgrim of the roads So he became a pilgrim instead. For seven years he walked thousands of kilometres across Europe, to Loreto, Assisi, Einsiedeln, Santiago de Compostela and the great shrines of Italy and France, sleeping outside, wearing rags, eating what he was given and giving most of it away. He spent his last years in Rome , sleeping in a niche in the ruins of the Colosseum and praying all day in churches, especially at the Forty Hours' adoration. Romans called him "the saint of the Forty Hours" and "the beggar of the Colosseum". Death in Holy Week He collapsed on the steps of Santa Maria dei Monti on Wednesday of Holy Week 1783 and died in a nearby butcher's house. Children ran through the streets crying "The saint is dead!" Over 130 miracles were reported in the following months. History. His life was written by his confessor, Fr Marconi, soon after his death, and is well documented. He is a reminder that holiness can be found among the homeles

d: Visionary, composer, healer, Doctor of the Church
x: Home › Saints St Hildegard of Bingen Visionary, composer, healer, Doctor of the Church Hildegard von Bingen by Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1098–1179, Rhineland (Germany) Feast day 17 September Canonised 2012, Benedict XVI (equivalent canonisation) The story Hildegard was the tenth child of a noble family and was given to the Church at eight, living with the anchoress Jutta at Disibodenberg. She became abbess in 1136 and later founded her own convents at Rupertsberg , by Bingen, and Eibingen , across the Rhine. The full story The visions From childhood she saw what she called "the shade of the living light". At 42 she felt commanded to write her visions down. The result was Scivias ("Know the Ways"), illustrated with extraordinary images, which Pope Eugene III read aloud at the Synod of Trier in 1147–48, approving her work. She wrote two more great visionary books. A woman of many talents She composed some 70 chants and the first known morality play with music, Ordo Virtutum . She wrote on medicine and natural science ( Physica , Causae et Curae ), invented a secret language ( Lingua Ignota ), corresponded with popes, emperors and St Bernard, and went on four preaching tours, unusual for a woman of her time. History. Hildegard is one of the best-documented women of the Middle Ages, through her own writings and letters. Some modern "Hildegard medicine" goes far beyond what she actually wrote. Path to sainthood Long venerated as a sai

d: The hermit who sailed across the Strait of Messina on his cloak
x: Home › Saints St Francis of Paola The hermit who sailed across the Strait of Messina on his cloak Ulisse giocchi, San Francesco di Paola attraversa lo stretto di Messina sul suo by Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1416–1507, Calabria and France Feast day 2 April Canonised 1519, Leo X The story Francis was born in Paola , Calabria, and named after St Francis of Assisi, to whom his parents had prayed for a child. At 15 he became a hermit in a cave by the sea. Followers joined him, and he founded the Order of Minims ("the least"), who keep a perpetual Lenten fast, abstaining from meat, eggs and dairy. The full story The cloak The best-known story says that in 1464 Francis wanted to cross to Sicily, but a boatman refused to take him because he could not pay. Francis spread his cloak on the water, tied one end to his staff as a sail, and sailed across the Strait of Messina with two companions. The scene is painted in many southern Italian churches, and Pius XII named him patron of Italian seafarers. The king's hermit His fame as a healer reached Louis XI of France , who was dying and begged the Pope to send him. Francis went reluctantly in 1483, did not cure the king but helped him die well, and stayed in France as adviser to Charles VIII and Louis XII. He died at Plessis-lès-Tours on Good Friday 1507, aged 91. History and legend. His life, his order and his time in France are historical, well documented in his canonisation process (begun 1512). d: Wonder-worker of the North, warmed by otters
x: Home › Saints St Cuthbert Wonder-worker of the North, warmed by otters Cuthbert discovers piece of timber - Life of St. Cuthbert (late 12th C), f.45v - by Bede, CC0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 634–687, Northumbria Feast day 20 March Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Cuthbert was a shepherd boy who, one night in 651, saw a light in the sky like angels carrying a soul to heaven; it was the night St Aidan died. He became a monk at Melrose , then prior of Lindisfarne , then a hermit on the Inner Farne , and finally, unwillingly, bishop of Lindisfarne. He died on Inner Farne on 20 March 687. (See our St Cuthbert's Way pages.) The full story The otters St Bede tells that while staying at Coldingham, Cuthbert went down to the sea at night and stood in the cold water up to his neck, praying until dawn. A monk who followed him secretly saw that when he came out, two otters bounded up, warmed his feet with their breath and dried them with their fur, then slipped back into the sea. Cuthbert, guessing he had been seen, asked the monk to tell no one until after his death. The incorrupt body When his tomb was opened in 698 , eleven years after his death, his body was found incorrupt. Fleeing the Vikings, the monks carried it around the North for over a century, until it came to rest at Durham in 995, where the great cathedral was built over it. His coffin, pectoral cross and the St Cuthbert Gospel (now in the British Library) survive. History and legend. Cuthbert is well documente

d: The archbishop who grabbed the devil by the nose
x: Home › Saints St Dunstan The archbishop who grabbed the devil by the nose Cartouche St Dunstan by Joel Gascoyne (c.1650-c.1704), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 909–988, England Feast day 19 May Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Dunstan was born near Glastonbury , educated by Irish monks there, and served at the court of King Athelstan. He became abbot of Glastonbury in 943, restored monastic life there under the Rule of St Benedict, and as Archbishop of Canterbury (959–988) led the great reform of the English Church under King Edgar. He was also a musician, illuminator and skilled metalworker. The full story The tongs The famous legend says that while Dunstan was working at his forge, the devil came to tempt him, disguised as a beautiful woman (or a man asking for a job). Dunstan noticed hooves under the robe, pulled his tongs red-hot from the fire, and seized the devil by the nose. The devil's howls were heard for miles around. The horseshoe In another tale the devil asked Dunstan to shoe his hoof. Dunstan nailed a horseshoe on so painfully that the devil begged for mercy and promised never to enter a house with a horseshoe over the door. This is said to be the origin of the lucky horseshoe. History and legend. Dunstan's career as reformer and archbishop is well documented. The devil stories appear in later lives and are legend, perhaps inspired by his skill as a metalworker. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint; the most popular English saint until Th

d: Viking king and patron of Norway
x: Home › Saints St Olav Viking king and patron of Norway Norwegian: Olav den helliges fall i slaget på Stiklestadtitle QS:P1476,no:"Olav by Peter Nicolai Arbo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 995–1030, Norway Feast day 29 July Recognised Pre-Congregation; declared a saint 1031 The story Olav Haraldsson was a Viking raider in England, France and the Baltic who was baptised in Rouen about 1013. He became King of Norway in 1015 and set about making it a Christian kingdom, building churches and introducing Christian laws, often by force. Driven out by Cnut the Great in 1028, he returned in 1030 and was killed at the battle of Stiklestad on 29 July 1030. The full story The saint king A year later, in 1031, his body was dug up and found incorrupt, with hair and nails grown. Bishop Grimkell declared him a saint. Miracles were reported at his grave in Nidaros (Trondheim), where Nidaros Cathedral was built over it, and pilgrims came from all over the North along the routes now revived as St Olav's Ways (see our St Olav's Way pages). Legends Norwegian folklore is full of Olav: he is said to have fought trolls, made springs gush where he struck the ground, and carved paths through mountains. He is shown with an axe, the weapon of his death, standing on a dragon or troll. History and legend. His reign, conversion policy and death are historical, known from skaldic poems and Snorri Sturluson's sagas. The troll stories are folklore. Path to sainthood Declared a saint by local bish

d: The girl who burst out of a dragon
x: Home › Saints St Margaret of Antioch The girl who burst out of a dragon German: Hl. Margarete Saint Margaret and the Dragontitle QS:P1476,de:"Hl. Margar by Raphael, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 304, Antioch in Pisidia Feast day 20 July Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Margaret (Marina in the East) was, according to legend, the daughter of a pagan priest at Antioch in Pisidia (today Turkey). Driven out for being a Christian, she kept sheep with her nurse. The Roman prefect Olybrius wanted to marry her; when she refused and declared herself a Christian, he had her tortured and imprisoned. The full story The dragon In prison the devil came to her as a huge dragon and swallowed her. But the cross she was holding irritated the dragon's insides (or grew larger), and it burst open, and Margaret stepped out unharmed. Because she came out of the dragon safe and sound, she became the patron of childbirth . She was later beheaded. A voice for Joan Margaret was one of the most popular saints of the Middle Ages and one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers. She was one of the three saints whose voices St Joan of Arc said she heard. Legend. Even the medieval Golden Legend called the dragon story "apocryphal and not to be believed". Because there is no historical evidence for her life, her feast was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969, although she remains in the Roman Martyrology. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint; feast removed from the universal calenda

d: Locked in a tower; patron of artillery and miners
x: Home › Saints St Barbara Locked in a tower; patron of artillery and miners Saint Barbara by Master Bolfgangus, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 3rd century, traditionally Nicomedia or Heliopolis Feast day 4 December Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Barbara was, in legend, the beautiful daughter of a rich pagan, Dioscorus , who locked her in a tower to keep her from suitors. While he was away she became a Christian and had a third window put in the bath house he was building, in honour of the Holy Trinity. The full story The lightning When her father discovered her faith, he denounced her to the governor. She was tortured, and her father himself beheaded her on a mountain. On the way down he was struck by lightning and burned to ashes. So she became patron of everyone who works with sudden fire and explosions: artillerymen, miners, firefighters and explosives workers. The powder magazine on a Spanish or Italian warship is still called the santabárbara . Barbara branches In Germany and Central Europe, cherry branches cut on her feast, 4 December, and put in water are expected to blossom by Christmas, the "Barbara branches" ( Barbarazweige ), a sign of new life in winter. Legend. Her story is late and legendary, and there is no early evidence of her life. Her feast was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969, but she remains in the Martyrology and is very popular in the Eastern Churches and in mining regions. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint; feast

d: The singing martyr, found incorrupt in 1599
x: Home › Saints St Cecilia The singing martyr, found incorrupt in 1599 Stefano Maderno - Martyrdom of Saint Cecilia - Church of St. Cecilia - Rome by real name: Jacek Durski pl.wiki: Durski commons: Durski e-mail: jacek , CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 230, Rome Feast day 22 November Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Cecilia was a Roman martyr buried in the Catacomb of St Callixtus , and her name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass. According to her 5th-century Acts , she was a noble Christian girl married against her will to Valerian . On her wedding night she told him an angel guarded her virginity; he converted, with his brother Tiburtius, and both were martyred. The full story Singing in her heart Her Acts say that as the wedding music played, "Cecilia sang in her heart to the Lord alone". From this line, misread as playing an organ, she became the patron of music . Condemned, she was shut in the steam bath of her house to suffocate, but survived. An executioner struck her neck three times and failed to cut off her head; she lived three days, giving her goods to the poor and asking that her house become a church. 1599 Her body was moved to Santa Cecilia in Trastevere in the 9th century. When the tomb was opened in 1599 , it was reported to be incorrupt, lying on its side, with the face turned down. The sculptor Stefano Maderno carved the beautiful marble statue of her in exactly that position, now under the altar. History or legend? Her early cult and bu

d: The lamb of Rome, martyred at twelve
x: Home › Saints St Agnes The lamb of Rome, martyred at twelve Saint Agnes with the Lamb – Copy by Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 291–304, Rome Feast day 21 January Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Agnes was a young girl of about 12 or 13 who was martyred in Rome, probably in the persecution of Diocletian, for refusing marriage and the worship of the gods. She is named in the Roman Canon. St Ambrose , Pope Damasus and the poet Prudentius all wrote about her within a century of her death. The full story Her story The tradition says she was sent to a brothel, but her hair grew miraculously to cover her, and a man who tried to touch her was struck blind (she prayed and he was healed). She was condemned to burn, but the flames parted, and she was killed with a sword to the throat. Ambrose wrote: "a new kind of martyrdom: too young to be punished, yet old enough for a crown." The lambs Her name is like the Latin agnus , "lamb". Every year on her feast, two lambs are blessed in the Basilica of Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura. Their wool is woven by nuns into the pallia , the woollen bands given by the Pope to new archbishops on 29 June. History and legend. Her martyrdom and young age are historical. The details of the brothel and the hair are legend added later. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint. Patronages Girls, chastity, engaged couples, victims of sexual abuse. d: The bishop who saved a boy choking on a fish bone
x: Home › Saints St Blaise The bishop who saved a boy choking on a fish bone Saint Blaisetitle QS:P1476,en:"Saint Blaise"label QS:Len,"Saint Blaise" by Pere Fernández Documented in Girona 1519-1521 Born in Murcia. Details , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived d. c. 316, Sebaste (Armenia) Feast day 3 February Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Blaise was bishop of Sebaste in Armenia (today Sivas, Turkey) and was martyred in the early 4th century, probably under the emperor Licinius. His Acts are late and legendary, but his cult spread widely in East and West. The full story The fish bone The legend says that Blaise, hiding in a cave from persecution, was visited by wild animals that he healed. When he was arrested and led to prison, a mother brought her son, who was choking on a fish bone . Blaise prayed over him and the boy was cured. A poor woman whose pig had been taken by a wolf got it back through his prayers; she later brought candles to his cell. The blessing of throats So on his feast, 3 February, Catholics receive the blessing of throats : the priest holds two crossed candles to the throat and prays, "Through the intercession of St Blaise, bishop and martyr, may God deliver you from every disease of the throat and from every other illness." He was martyred by being torn with iron wool combs, then beheaded. History and legend. His existence as a martyr bishop is accepted, but his Acts date from centuries later. Path to sainthood Pre-Congregation saint. Patronage

d: Martyr at eleven, who forgave her killer
x: Home › Saints St Maria Goretti Martyr at eleven, who forgave her killer Santuario di Santa Maria Goretti 7 by Accurimbono, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1890–1902, Lazio (Italy) Feast day 6 July Canonised 1950, Pius XII The story Maria Goretti was born in Corinaldo in the Marche in 1890 to a poor farming family who moved to the Pontine marshes south of Rome, near Nettuno . Her father died of malaria when she was nine, and she looked after the house and her siblings while her mother worked the fields. The full story 5 July 1902 The family shared a house with the Serenelli family. Alessandro Serenelli , 20, had repeatedly tried to seduce her. On 5 July 1902, when she was alone, he tried to rape her. She resisted, saying it was a sin and he would go to hell. He stabbed her 14 times. She died the next day in hospital, after forgiving him: "I want him to be with me in Paradise." Alessandro's conversion Serenelli was sentenced to 30 years. Unrepentant at first, he said Maria appeared to him in a dream in prison, giving him lilies, and he changed. After his release in 1929 he asked her mother's forgiveness; she forgave him, and they went to Mass together that Christmas. He was present in St Peter's Square at her canonisation in 1950, with her mother, and spent the rest of his life as a lay brother with the Capuchins. History. Her story is fully documented, including the trial and Serenelli's own testimony. The prison dream is his own account. Path to sainthood Beatified

d: Visionary of Lourdes, still incorrupt
x: Home › Saints St Bernadette Soubirous Visionary of Lourdes, still incorrupt Bernadette Soubirous by abbé P. Bernadou, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1844–1879, Lourdes and Nevers (France) Feast day 16 April (18 February in France) Canonised 1933, Pius XI The story Bernadette was the eldest child of a miller ruined by poverty, living in the town's former prison cell, the cachot , in Lourdes . Sickly with asthma and barely able to read, on 11 February 1858 , aged 14, she was gathering firewood at the grotto of Massabielle when she saw "a lady" dressed in white with a blue sash and yellow roses at her feet. The full story The apparitions The Lady appeared 18 times between February and July 1858. She asked for prayer and penance, told Bernadette to dig in the ground, where a spring appeared that still flows, and asked for a chapel to be built and processions to come. On 25 March she gave her name in the local dialect: " Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou " ("I am the Immaculate Conception"), a phrase Bernadette did not understand. The bishop recognised the apparitions in 1862. (See our Lourdes page.) Nevers Bernadette refused all attention. In 1866 she joined the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she worked as a nurse and sacristan and suffered tuberculosis of the bone. "I am like a broom: the Virgin used me, then put me back in my corner." She died on 16 April 1879, aged 35. History. The apparitions were investigated by Church and civil authorities at the time; Ber

d: The priest who became a leper with his people
x: Home › Saints St Damien of Molokai The priest who became a leper with his people Father Damien, photograph by William Brigham by William Brigham, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1840–1889, Belgium and Hawaii Feast day 10 May Canonised 2009, Benedict XVI The story Jozef De Veuster was born in Tremelo, Belgium, and joined the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts , taking the name Damien. He went to Hawaii in his brother's place in 1864 and was ordained in Honolulu. The full story Kalaupapa In 1866 the Hawaiian government began exiling people with leprosy (Hansen's disease) to the remote Kalaupapa peninsula on Molokai, cut off by 600 m cliffs. In 1873 Damien volunteered to go. He found some 800 people living in misery. He built houses, a church, a hospital and coffins, dug graves, dressed wounds, taught farming and organised a choir and a band, and demanded supplies from the government. He began his sermons "We lepers". "I am one of them" In 1884, he noticed he could not feel boiling water on his foot: he had leprosy. He kept working, helped by St Marianne Cope and her Franciscan sisters, and died on 15 April 1889, aged 49. When a Presbyterian minister attacked his memory, Robert Louis Stevenson , who had visited Molokai, wrote a famous open letter in his defence. History. Damien's life is fully documented by his own letters and many witnesses. Path to sainthood Beatified 1995 by John Paul II; canonised 11 October 2009 by Benedict XVI. d: Don Bosco, juggler for God, and Grigio the guardian dog
x: Home › Saints St John Bosco Don Bosco, juggler for God, and Grigio the guardian dog Verona, chiesa di San Giovanni Bosco - Pala d'altare by Syrio, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1815–1888, Piedmont (Italy) Feast day 31 January Canonised 1934, Pius XI The story John Bosco was born to a poor farming family at Becchi, near Turin. At nine he had a dream in which wild animals turned into lambs, and a lady told him he must win over unruly boys "not with blows but with gentleness". As a boy he learned to juggle, do magic tricks and walk a tightrope to draw a crowd, then repeated the Sunday sermon to them. The full story The Oratory Ordained in 1841, he found Turin full of homeless boys working in factories, sleeping rough or in prison. He gathered them in an oratory in Valdocco, gave them food, schooling and trades, and played with them. In 1859 he founded the Salesians (named after St Francis de Sales) and, with St Mary Mazzarello, the Salesian Sisters. His "preventive system" of education rested on reason, religion and loving kindness. Grigio Don Bosco had enemies, and was attacked several times on the dark roads near Valdocco. From about 1852, a large grey dog, which he called Grigio ("Greyish"), appeared out of nowhere when he was in danger, drove off attackers, would not let him leave the house when danger waited outside, and then vanished. It never ate, and no one knew where it came from. Bosco wrote about it in his Memoirs and said it was strange, but true. Histor

d: The saint of joy, Apostle of Rome
x: Home › Saints St Philip Neri The saint of joy, Apostle of Rome Philip Neri in Ecstasy by Guido Reni - Chiesa Nuova - Rome 2015 by José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived 1515–1595, Florence and Rome Feast day 26 May Canonised 1622, Gregory XV The story Philip Neri was a Florentine who gave up a business career and came to Rome around 1533. He lived simply, studied, and spent nights praying in the catacombs. At Pentecost 1544, in the catacomb of St Sebastian, he felt a ball of fire enter his heart; after his death his heart was found to be enlarged and two ribs broken. The full story The Oratory Ordained in 1551, he gathered young men for conversation, prayer, music and charity in a room ( oratorio ) at San Girolamo; the music sung there gave its name to the oratorio as a musical form. He founded the Congregation of the Oratory in 1575, centred at the Chiesa Nuova . He also began the walking pilgrimage to Rome's Seven Churches , a kind of joyful picnic-procession. Holy humour Philip used jokes to keep people (and himself) humble. He wore his clothes inside out, shaved half his beard, read joke books before cardinals, and made a proud young nobleman walk through Rome with a fox tail pinned to his back. To a gossip he gave a famous penance: to pluck a chicken in the street, then go back and gather every feather, which is impossible, like taking back gossip. "A joyful heart is more easily made perfect than a downcast one." History. Philip's life is very well documen

d: Disciple of St John, burned at 86
x: Home › Saints St Polycarp Disciple of St John, burned at 86 Saint Polycarpe au bûcher by Octave 444, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 69–155, Smyrna (Turkey) Feast day 23 February Recognised Pre-Congregation The story Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna (today İzmir). St Irenaeus, who heard him preach as a boy, says he had known St John the Apostle and others who had seen the Lord. St Ignatius of Antioch wrote him a letter on his way to martyrdom, and Polycarp's own Letter to the Philippians survives. The full story 86 years The Martyrdom of Polycarp , written by the church of Smyrna soon after his death, is the oldest account of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament. Arrested at a farm, the old bishop fed his captors and asked for an hour to pray. In the stadium the proconsul urged him to swear by Caesar and curse Christ. He answered: " Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me? " The fire He was sentenced to burn. He asked not to be nailed to the stake. The account says the flames formed an arch around him like a sail, and he did not burn, but "was like bread baking"; a fragrant scent rose. An executioner stabbed him, and so much blood flowed that it quenched the fire. The Christians gathered his bones, "more precious than jewels", and kept the day of his death as his "birthday" each year, the beginning of the cult of martyrs. History. The Martyrdom is an eyewitness letter and largely historica

The full story The roses The best-known legend says Elizabeth was carrying bread in her cloak to the poor when she met her husband (or her disapproving in-laws), who asked what she was hiding. When she opened her cloak, there were only roses , in the middle of winter. The same story is told of her great-niece, St Elizabeth of Portugal . Widowhood Ludwig died on crusade in 1227. Elizabeth, at 20, left the Wartburg with her children, became a Franciscan tertiary, and gave her dowry to found a hospital at Marburg , where she nursed the sick, including lepers, with her own hands, under the harsh direction of her confessor, Conrad of Marburg. The full story Shepherd at Sebourg He worked as a shepherd for a woman in Sebourg , near Valenciennes, for six years. Villagers said he was seen tending his sheep and praying at Mass at the same time, giving rise to a saying, "I'm not St Drogo; I can't ring the bells and walk in the procession." Walled in On a pilgrimage he was struck by a disfiguring illness (perhaps a hernia or a hideous growth) that frightened people. Legend. His life is known from a short Vita written soon after his death, but it is full of legend. His cult remains strong locally in Sebourg. d: Carried to Rome in chains, begging not to be rescued from the lions
x: Home › Saints St Ignatius of Antioch Carried to Rome in chains, begging not to be rescued from the lions Ignatius Theophorus, Ignatius of Antioch · Wikivorker · CC0, via Wikimedia Commons Lived c. 35–c. 107, Antioch (Syria) – Rome Feast day 17 October Recognised Pre-Congregation; Apostolic Father The story Ignatius, bishop of Antioch — tradition calls him a disciple of John the Apostle — was arrested under Trajan and sent under guard of ten soldiers ('my ten leopards') across Asia Minor and Greece to die in Rome. Unlike most martyrs we do not depend only on later legend: seven letters in his own voice survive from the road. The full story Letters on the road to death At Smyrna and Troas he wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia and Smyrna, and to Polycarp. The letters burn with three themes: unity around the bishop, the real flesh-and-blood reality of Christ against docetism, and an almost frightening desire for martyrdom. To Rome he pleaded: do not free me — 'I am God's wheat, to be ground by the teeth of beasts, that I may be found pure bread of Christ.' The arena He was killed by wild beasts in Rome, probably under Trajan (c. 107; some scholars argue a little later). Eusebius preserves the outline; the vivid arena details come from later Acts . His bones, tradition says, were gathered and carried back to Antioch, and later translated to St Clement's in Rome. History. The full story Barefoot duchess Her Vita describes a deliberate downward mobility: plain dress, barefoot walks even in Silesian winter (carrying shoes in her hand to satisfy critics, which rather misses — and makes — the point), a hairshirt late in life, and long prayer before a small ivory Madonna she carried everywhere. Widow among ruins Henry died in 1238; their son Henry the Pious fell against the Mongols at Legnica in 1241, where Hedwig is said to have identified his body among the dead. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius, describes the pogrom of 249 under Decius' predecessor: an aged virgin Apollonia was seized by a mob. The full story Eusebius' letter Dionysius writes that they broke her jaw and teeth with blows and threatened to burn her alive unless she blasphemed. Given a moment to think, she threw herself into the fire — a detail early Christians themselves debated (Augustine discusses whether such self-offering is lawful) and which art softened into execution. History The word comes from the Latin adventus , "coming". A season of preparation before Christmas appears in Gaul and Spain in the late 4th and 5th centuries: the Council of Saragossa (380) asked the faithful to be in church daily from 17 December to Epiphany, and Bishop Perpetuus of Tours (d. 490) set a fast from St Martin's Day (11 November), which was nicknamed "St Martin's Lent". Rome kept a shorter season, and Pope Gregory the Great (590–604) is credited with fixing it at four Sundays, the form the West still keeps (Catholic Encyclopedia, "Advent"). Why it is observed Advent looks two ways. It prepares for the celebration of Christ's first coming at Bethlehem, and it turns the Church toward his promised return in glory. That is why the first Sunday's Gospel is about the end of the age, the middle Sundays belong to John the Baptist, and the fourth Sunday finally arrives at Mary and the Annunciation. The mood is expectant and hopeful, more like waiting at a window than fasting in the desert. The East kept 6 January for both birth and Epiphany, and gradually took up 25 December in the late 4th century; St John Chrysostom preached in Antioch in 386 that the December feast had reached them only a few years before. It is older than Christmas: Clement of Alexandria (c. 200) mentions Egyptian Christians keeping Christ's baptism on 6 January. Ancient Western texts join three manifestations: the star to the Magi, the voice at the Jordan, and the water made wine at Cana (Catholic Encyclopedia, "Epiphany"). Why it is observed Christmas shows that Christ is born; Epiphany shows who he is and for whom . The Magi are the first Gentiles to worship him, so the feast is about the whole world being drawn to Christ, and the weeks after it read his first signs and calls. History A fast before Easter is very ancient. The Council of Nicaea (325) already speaks of "the forty days" ( tessarakoste ), and St Athanasius's Festal Letters of the 330s urge the Egyptian Church to keep them. The number recalls Moses on Sinai, Elijah's journey to Horeb and above all Christ's forty days in the wilderness. Lent was also the final preparation of catechumens for baptism at Easter, which is why its Gospels (the Samaritan woman, the man born blind, Lazarus) are baptismal. Ashes on the first day were at first given to public penitents; by the 11th century everyone received them (Catholic Encyclopedia, "Lent"). Why it is observed Lent is forty days of return: prayer, fasting and almsgiving (Matthew 6), to clear room for God and for the poor, and to walk with Christ toward his Passion. Pope St Leo the Great's Lenten sermons (5th century) describe it as a yearly renewal of the whole Church. History Pentekoste is Greek for "fiftieth". It was first the Jewish harvest Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), fifty days after Passover, which in later Jewish tradition also remembered the giving of the Law at Sinai. On that feast the Holy Spirit came on the apostles in wind and fire (Acts 2). Tertullian (c. 200) already names Pentecost as a solemn time for baptism; in England it was called Whitsunday from the white robes of the newly baptized (Catholic Encyclopedia, "Pentecost"). Why it is observed Pentecost completes Easter: the Risen Christ pours out the Spirit, and the Church goes out to every nation. The crowd hearing one message in many languages reverses the scattering at Babel. It is often called the birthday of the Church. Colours and symbols Red for fire, the dove , tongues of flame , wind, the sequence Veni Sancte Spiritus and the hymn Veni Creator Spiritus (9th century, attributed to Rabanus Maurus), red flowers, and readings in several languages. Catholic practice Pentecost is a solemnity closing the Easter season, often with a vigil Mass. The Paschal candle moves to the baptistery. Confirmations are common in this season. x: Home Music of the Church Year Bach and Handel, spirituals, holy blues, gospel and mountain hymns Every season of the Church year has its music, and Christian music in America has come down several streams that keep meeting. Handel and Bach wrote for the liturgy of their own churches. African Americans made the spirituals from the Bible stories they heard, hiding hope of freedom inside the Exodus and the Cross. From the spirituals and the work songs came both the blues and gospel : the same flattened "blue" notes, the same call and response, the same moan, one sung on Saturday night and one on Sunday morning. Many blues singers were preachers' sons or preachers themselves, and the father of gospel, Thomas A. Dorsey, had been a blues pianist. Meanwhile, in the Appalachian hills, shape-note singing and mountain hymns became country gospel and bluegrass , and these streams crossed again and again, as when a Black guitarist named Lesley Riddle taught the Carter Family his songs. All of it, from Leipzig to Clarksdale to Clinch Mountain, sings the same Scriptures.
